Surat al-Waqi'ah

It is Meccan, as al-Bayhaqi related in *al-Dala'il* and others transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn al-Zubayr. Some scholars excepted His saying: ﴿A company of the earlier generations﴾ and ﴿and a company of the later ones﴾ [56:39-40], as reported in *al-Itqan* (al-Suyuti's *al-Itqan fi 'Ulum al-Qur'an*). Likewise His saying: ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars…﴾ up to ﴿…that you deny?﴾ [56:75-82] was excepted, on account of what Muslim recorded regarding its occasion of revelation, which will come, God willing. In *Majma' al-Bayan* there is a report of the exception of His saying: ﴿And you make your provision that you deny?﴾ [56:82], from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah. Its number of verses is ninety-nine according to the Hijazi and Syrian counts, ninety-seven according to the Basran count, and ninety-six according to the Kufan count. The details of this are in the place prepared for such matters. It and Surat al-Rahman are akin in that each contains a description of the Resurrection, Paradise and Hell.

Abu Hayyan (in *al-Bahr*) said: its connection to what precedes it is that it included the punishment of the criminals and the bliss of the believers. God distinguished between the two gardens of some believers and the two gardens of others, so the responsible people were divided into disbeliever, excellent believer and lesser believer. On this basis the opening of this surah came with their being "companions of the right hand," "companions of the left hand," and "the foremost."

Some eminent scholars said: observe the connection of His saying ﴿When the Event occurs﴾ [56:1] with His saying ﴿Then when the heaven splits open﴾ [55:37]. In al-Rahman He mentioned only the splitting of the sky, and in al-Waqi'ah only the shaking of the earth. It is as if the two surahs, because of their mutual entailment and their unity, are one surah, so each mentions in itself a part of everything. He reversed the order: he mentioned at the beginning of this one what is at the end of that one, and at the end of this one what is at the beginning of that one. He opened Surat al-Rahman by mentioning the Qur'an, then the sun and the moon, then the plants, then the creation of man and the jinn, then the description of the Day of Resurrection, then the description of Hell, then the description of Paradise. This surah begins with mention of the Resurrection, then the description of Paradise, then the description of Hell, then the creation of man, then the plants, then the water, then the fire. Then it mentions the stars, which are not mentioned in al-Rahman, just as the sun and the moon are not mentioned here. Then it mentions the Balance. Thus this surah is like a counterpart to that one, and like something that includes the return of the last part to the first (*radd al-'ajz 'ala al-sadr*).

Reports about its virtue have also come.

Abu 'Ubayd in *Fada'il al-Qur'an*, Ibn al-Daris, al-Harith ibn Abi Usamah, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: Whoever recites Surat al-Waqi'ah every night, poverty will never afflict him."

Ibn 'Asakir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas something similar, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) (*marfu'an*). Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Anas, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: "Surat al-Waqi'ah is the surah of wealth, so recite it and teach it to your children."

[Page 129]

Al-Daylami transmitted from him, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) (*marfu'an*): "Teach your women Surat al-Waqi'ah, for it is the surah of wealth."

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿When the Event occurs﴾, that is, when the Resurrection happens, with *waqa'at* (occurred) meaning *hadathat* (happened). *Al-Waqi'ah* (the Event) is a proper name by predominance, or a name transferred to the Resurrection. Ibn 'Abbas explicitly stated that it is among its names. It was so named to announce the certainty of its occurrence, as if it were an event that is occurring in itself, regardless of the occurrence that falls within the conditional clause. So the attribution here is not like in "my neighbor came, the one who came," for that is redundant (*laghw*), since each verb indicates an agent that is not specified.

Al-Dahhak said: *al-Waqi'ah* is the *sayhah* (the Cry), which is the blast of the Trumpet (*al-nafkhah fi al-Sur*). It was also said that *al-Waqi'ah* is the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis, which will fall on the Day of Resurrection, but this is nothing (of substance).

*Idha* (when) is an adverbial of time that carries the meaning of a conditional, as is apparent. Its governing element, according to Abu Hayyan, is the verb following it. Thus it is in the accusative position, governed by *waqa'at*, like all other conditional nouns, and it is not annexed to the clause. The majority hold that it is annexed to the clause. It was said that here it has been stripped of its adverbial sense and functions as a direct object (*maf'ul bihi*), with no omitted object. It was also said: it has not been stripped of that meaning, and it is in the accusative governed by *laysa* (the verb "is not"). The wording of al-Zamakhshari suggests his preference for this view.

It was also said: it is governed by an omitted element, which is the response (*jawab*), meaning: ﴿When the Event occurs﴾, such-and-such will be the case. In *al-Kashf* it is said: this is the eloquent and sound view, since the accusative governed by an implied "remember" (*idhkur*) is common with *idh*, while governance by *laysa* is valid only if *idha* is taken as purely adverbial. Abu Hayyan objected to the accusative governed by *laysa*, saying that no grammarian holds this view, because *laysa* in negation is like *ma*, and *ma* does not govern. Likewise *laysa*, since it is stripped of the indication of event and time. The claim that it is a verb in a metaphorical sense, with the adverb governed by the event that occurs within it, means that where there is no event in it there is no governance in it. Then he mentioned a view similar to what the author of *al-Kashf* mentioned, regarding the obligation of the *fa'* (the particle "then") with *laysa* when it is not stripped of the conditional meaning. He objected to the claim that *ma* does not govern, saying that the grammarians have explicitly permitted the adverb to be related to it, by interpreting it as *intafa* (has been negated), and that the aroma of the verb suffices for it, and *laysa* is analogized to it in this respect. Likewise the claim of the obligation of *fa'* with *laysa* when *idha* is not stripped of the conditional meaning: the obligation of the *fa'* with defective verbs of this kind applies only to the response of the conditional particle *in*, because of its governance, as they explicitly stated. As for *idha*, the entry of the *fa'* into its response is contrary to the original rule.

Two other views concerning it will come, God willing. After the discussion and debate, the first view is that the governing element is omitted, and it is the response, as you have heard. In leaving it unspecified there is awe and magnification of the matter of the Event.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 56, verse 2:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿There is no denying of its occurrence.﴾ It is either a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ, a clause inserted between sentence elements) that affirms the certainty of its occurrence, or a circumstantial clause (ḥal) describing "the Event" (al-wāqi'a), as Ibn ʿAṭiyya said. "Kādhiba" (denying) is an active participle (ism fā'il) functioning as an adjective of an omitted noun, meaning "a soul" (nafs). It was also said to mean "a statement" (muqāla), but the first is preferable, because describing a person as a liar is more common than describing a report as false. "Al-wāqi'a" (the Event) means a violent fall, and the word became common for the occurrence of a great matter. It may also be specifically applied to war, which is why it is used here. The lām is for specifying a time (lām al-tawqīt), like it is in your saying: "I wrote it five nights had passed," meaning: at the time of its occurrence there will be no soul that denies, in the sense that it lies against God, Exalted is He, and lies in denying His report about it. The clarification is that one who denies the Hour now is denying Him, Exalted is He, regarding its occurrence, and he is lying in his denial of Him, Glorified is He, because it is a report contrary to what is real. When it occurs, he will no longer be a liar denying, but a truthful one confirming. It was also said: the meaning is that at the time of its occurrence, no soul will be lying about anything whatsoever. Its soundness, however, is based on the view that no lie will issue from anyone on the Day of Resurrection, and that the statement of the people, ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23], is answered by what is mentioned in its proper place. Or the lām is kept in its literal sense. And "kādhiba" is also an adjective of that omitted noun, meaning: ﴿There is no denying of its occurrence﴾ by any soul, in the sense that no one will deny its occurrence, nor will anyone say to the Hour, "You did not happen," because existence has been confirmed, just as one says to it in this world, by the tongue of speech or action, for whoever is deceived by the adornments of this world has denied the Hour in its occurrence

by the tongue of state, "You will never happen." This is like your saying to your addressee, "We have no king," and to someone well-known, "a liar," meaning: no one will call you a liar, saying, "It is not occurring." In it there is an allegorical metaphor (isti'āra tamthīliyya), because the Hour is not fit to be addressed except in that way, either by way of imagination (takhyīl), as when one says to fat, "Where are you going?", which is the more apparent, or in reality. He also permitted "kādhiba" to derive from the expression "my soul lied to him" (kadhabat nafsī) and "it made him lie" (kadhdhabathu), when wishes beguile him, bring distant matters close to him, and encourage him to undertake a great affair. As for the lām, it was said that it is also in its literal sense, meaning: when it occurs, no soul will have anything to tell its companion about enduring its severity and bearing it, and urging him toward it.

In al-Kashf, the lām in this aspect is for specifying time, as it is in the first aspect. He also permitted "kādhiba" to be a verbal noun (maṣdar) meaning "denial," which is "discouragement" (tathbīṭ), and the meaning of the lām is clear: there will be no turning back or return for its occurrence, like a truthful charge from one of overpowering might. Something similar has been related from al-Ḥasan and Qatada. It has been mentioned that the true meaning of denial in this sense returns to the soul denying its own lying, its urging, and its encouragement, and he recited as evidence for that the verse of Zuhayr:

A lion of Ba'tharr hunts men, when the lion lies to his peers, it speaks truthfully.

It is also permissible to make "al-kādhiba" mean "the lie," in the sense that there is no lie in the Event; rather, it is a truthful event that cannot be endured, like "a truthful charge" and "a charger who is truthful with it." Or in the sense that at the time of its occurrence it is not a lie, because it is a truth with no doubt in it. What has been mentioned appears more apparent than what preceded, even if something similar has been related from those you have heard. Yes, it was said against both: the verbal noun coming on the pattern of the active participle is rare.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 56, verse 3:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Abasing [some], exalting [others]﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is abasing for some peoples and exalting for others, as Ibn 'Abbas said, and a group transmitted it from him. The sentence serves to affirm its greatness and to inspire awe of its matter, for great events are characterized by abasing and exalting, as is observed in the change of dynasties and the emergence of trials, in the humbling of the mighty and the elevation of the lowly. The placing of abasing before exalting is for the intensification of awe. Or it is an explanation of what will happen on that Day of the lowering of the wretched to the depths and the raising of the happy to the ranks of the Gardens. On this is the saying of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "It abased the enemies of Allah to the Fire and raised the friends of Allah to the Garden." Or it is an explanation of what occurs of that and of the removal of celestial bodies from their places, the scattering of the stars, and the moving of mountains through the air like clouds. Ad-Dahhak, after interpreting the Event as the Blast, said: "Abasing: it lowers its force so that the near ones hear it. ﴿Exalting﴾: it raises it so that the far ones hear it." This was also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah. Abu 'Ali assumed the omitted subject joined with the particle fa', meaning: "so it is ﴿abasing﴾," and made the sentence the answer of "when" (idha), as if it were said: ﴿When the Event occurs﴾ it abases a people and exalts others. Zayd ibn 'Ali, al-Hasan, 'Isa, Abu Haywah, Ibn Abi 'Ablah, Ibn Muqsim, al-Za'farani, and al-Yazidi in his choice read "khafidatan rafi'atan" with the accusative on both. Their basis is that both be taken as circumstantial accusatives (hal) of the Event, on the understanding that ﴿there is no denier of its occurrence﴾ is a parenthetical clause, or as two circumstantial accusatives of its occurrence.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 56, verses 4–6:

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿When the earth is shaken with a violent shaking﴾, meaning it is quaked and moved with an intense movement, such that whatever buildings and mountains are upon it are demolished. [The phrase] "with a violent shaking" (rajjan) is connected to "lowering" (khafidah) or to "raising" (rafi'ah), by way of the grammatical principle of competing governors (min bab al-a'mal, i.e., tanazu' al-'amal). Or it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿When the Event occurs﴾, as many have said. Ibn Jinni and Abu al-Fadl al-Razzi said: ﴿When the earth is shaken﴾ is in the place of nominative case, as the predicate of the subject which is ﴿When the Event occurs﴾. Neither of them is a conditional clause; rather, [idha] means "a time," that is, the time of its occurrence, the time the earth is shaken. Ibn Malik claimed that (idha) can be a subject, and he cited this verse as evidence. Abu Hayyan said: it is a substitute for ﴿When the Event occurs﴾, and in my view the answer of the condition is explicitly stated, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then the companions of the right hand﴾. The meaning is: when such and such occurs, then the companions of the right hand, how fortunate they are, and how great is the reward with which they will be recompensed; that is, their felicity and the greatness of their ranks with God, the Mighty and Majestic, will become manifest at that time, the time of severe difficulty upon the world.

It was also said: they are driven and moved from their places, from bassa al-ghanam, when one drives the sheep. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and the mountains are set in motion﴾ [al-Naba' 20].

Zayd ibn 'Ali recited (rujjat, wa-bussat) in the active voice, meaning they shook and crumbled. In the speech of Hind bint al-Khass, describing a she-camel by signs that indicate her pregnancy:
Her eye is aroused, her hind-parts sway, and she walks and splays her legs.
﴿So it becomes﴾, that is, as a result it becomes ﴿scattered dust﴾, dust ﴿dispersed﴾, scattered. The intended meaning is any dust, according to most scholars. Ibn 'Abbas said it is what is stirred up with the rays of the sun when they enter through a window opening. In another report from him, it is what flies off from a fire when it blazes.

Al-Nakha'i recited (munbattan) with the letter ta' with two dots above, from al-batt, meaning cutting off. The intended meaning of it is what has been mentioned, from [the root] with the three-dotted letter (tha').

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 56, verse 7:

﴿And you were﴾ is an address to the present community and the earlier nations together, by way of taghlib (the dominance of one group in address over another), as much of the scholars have held. Some others said: it is an address to the present community only. Apparently the verb "kana" here also carries the meaning of "sara" (became), i.e., "and you became" ﴿spouses﴾, that is, kinds, ﴿three﴾. Every kind that is paired with another kind, either in existence or in mention, is called a zawj (spouse, pair). Al-Raghib said: "Zawj" is applied to each of two partners, male and female, among animals that mate, and to each of two partners within them; and in other things, such as a shoe and a sandal, and to everything that is joined with another, either similar to it or opposite to it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 56, verses 8–9:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then the companions of the right hand — what are the companions of the right hand!﴾ ﴿And the companions of the left hand — what are the companions of the left hand!﴾ is an elaboration of the three categories (azwaj), with a general indication of their states before their detailed description. The prevailing view among scholars is that "the companions of the right hand" is the subject (mubtada', the topic of the nominal sentence). His saying, ﴿what are the companions of the right hand﴾: "ma" here is interrogative, a second subject (mubtada' thani), and "the companions" (ashab) is its predicate (khabar). The whole sentence is the predicate of the first subject, and the explicit noun that stands in place of the pronoun (al-dhahir al-qa'im maqam al-damir) is the linking element. The same applies to His saying, ﴿and the companions of the left hand﴾, and so on. The original form in both places is "ma hum?", meaning "what are they in their condition and attributes?" Although "ma" is commonly used to ask about the essence and reality of a thing, it may also be used to ask about an attribute or a state, as when you say "ma Zayd?" and the answer is "a scholar" or "a physician."

The explicit noun was placed in the position of the pronoun because it brings in the intended meaning more fully: magnification (tafkhim) in the first case and reprehension (taf'idh) in the second. The purpose is to make the listener marvel at the greatness or the horror of the two groups, as if it were said: "The companions of the right hand are in the utmost good state, and the companions of the left hand are in the utmost wretched state."

It has also been said that the phrase "ma ashab..." is a predicate with an implied "say" (taqdir al-qawl), as is known when a performative sentence (jumla insha'iyya) functions as a predicate. That is, "what are the companions..." is said about them, so there is no need to treat it as the placing of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun. However, this view is open to question.

"Al-maymana" means the side of the right, or blessing and prosperity (al-yumn wa al-barakah). "Al-mash'ama" means the side of the left, from the "inauspicious hand" (al-yad al-shu'ma), which is the left, or it derives from ill omen (al-shu'm), the opposite of good fortune (al-yaman). It has been preferred to take both words to denote the side, because this fits better with what follows in the detailed description.

The scholars differed about the two groups. It has been said: the companions of the right hand are the people of high rank, and the companions of the left hand are the people of low rank, taking this from how they associate the right with good fortune and the left with bad, as you hear in the terms "sanih" and "barih" (omens). This is a common figurative usage (majaz shai'). It has also been permitted that it be a metonymy (kinaya). It has been said: they are those who are given their records in their right hands, and those who are given theirs in their left hands. It has been said: they are those who are taken by the right side to Paradise, and those who are taken by the left side to the Fire. It has been said:

the people of blessing and the people of ill omen, for the blessed are blessed in themselves through their obedience, and the wretched are ill-omened for themselves through their disobediences.

Al-Alusi's commentary on verse 56:12:

The phrase of His, the Exalted: ﴿in the Gardens of Bliss﴾ is related to ﴿those brought near﴾, or to an implied verb which is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from their pronoun, meaning: "being in the Gardens of Bliss." On both readings there is an indication that their nearness is pure pleasure and comfort, not like the nearness of the king's special courtiers who are occupied with his affairs in his presence, but rather like the nearness of his companions and boon-companions, who have no occupation and upon whom no command or prohibition descends. Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 56, verses 13–14:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿A company of the earlier generations﴾ is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada', the subject of a nominal sentence), i.e. "they are a company," and so on. It is permitted that it be a subject whose predicate is omitted, i.e. "from among them," or that it be a first or second predicate, "for those" (li-ula'ika). Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a subject whose predicate is ﴿on thrones﴾. The thullah (company) in the commonly known usage is a group, whether large or small. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is a community of many people from among the people, and he cited his saying:

*"There came to them a thullah of the Khindif tribe, with an army like a torrent of flood-water, foaming."*

His saying after it: ﴿and few﴾ and so on is sufficient proof of the largeness (of the thullah). The end of his words. The apparent meaning is that he cited the verse as evidence for the meaning of abundance in thullah. If the ba' (in the poem's phrasing, "bi-jaysh") is taqridiyya (a ba' of emphasis that strips the meaning of an intensive sense), which is the apparent case, then the matter is explicit. Otherwise, the inference for it is that the context is one of hyperbole and praise. As for his inference from what follows, that is because contrast (taqabul) is required, since thullah was not established by consensus to mean "few," so that what follows should be taken as a limitation. Rather, it is either for abundance, and derivation from it is more indicative, because thall means pouring out and also complete demolition, while thullah with a kasra means a large flock of sheep. Or it is for a general sense of group, like firqah (faction) and qit'ah (portion), from thall meaning breaking, as if it were a group broken off and cut away from the people. However, usage has predominated for it to mean the large number. So the meaning is: a large group of the earlier ones, namely the people who went before from Adam until our Prophet, upon both of them and upon the great prophets between them be blessings and peace. ﴿And few of the later ones﴾: they are the people from our Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, until the Hour arises. This does not contradict his saying, upon him be blessings and peace:

"Indeed my community will outnumber the other nations." That is, they will surpass them in number. This is because the greater number of the forerunners among the earlier peoples compared with the forerunners of this community does not prevent the greater number of the followers of these from the followers of those.

The result of this is that the whole of this community surpasses others in number, like a village in which there are ten scholars and a hundred commoners, and another in which there are five scholars and a thousand commoners. The elite of the first are more numerous than the elite of the second, and the commoners of the second and the total of its people are many times those of the first. It may not be said that the greater number of the followers of these is contradicted by His saying: ﴿A company of the earlier ones﴾ and ﴿a company of the later ones﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 39, 40], since it refers to the companions of the right (ashab al-yamin), who are the followers, and He expressed each with thullah, i.e. a large group. This is because we say: there is no indication in the verse of more than the description of each of the two groups as numerous, and that does not contradict the greater number of one of them. Thus it results that the forerunners of the former nations are more numerous than the forerunners of our community, and the followers of our community are more numerous than the followers of the (other) nations. By "nations" is meant what includes the prophets, and then it is not far-fetched to say: the abundance of the forerunners of the earlier ones is only through their prophets, so there is no objection to the forerunners of this community, for most of them are forerunners of nations together with their prophets, upon them be peace.

Imam Ahmad, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "When there was revealed ﴿A company of the earlier ones﴾ and ﴿and few of the later ones﴾, that was hard upon the companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, so there was revealed ﴿A company of the earlier ones﴾ and ﴿and a company of the later ones﴾. Then the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, said: 'Indeed I hope that you will be a third of the people of Paradise; rather, you are half of the people of Paradise' (or 'a moiety of the people of Paradise'), 'and you will share the second half with them.'" The apparent meaning is that the fewness of those described by it was hard upon them, and that the second verse removed that, lifted it, and replaced it with abundance. What supports this is what Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "When there was revealed ﴿A company of the earlier ones﴾ and ﴿and few of the later ones﴾, the companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ grieved

[p. 135]

and said: 'Then there will be of the community of Muhammad ﷺ only a few.' So at midday there was revealed ﴿A company of the earlier ones﴾ and ﴿and a company of the later ones﴾, and it abrogated ﴿and few of the later ones﴾." Al-Zamakhshari rejected this and said: the report is not sound, for two reasons.

The first is that the first verse concerns the foremost (al-sabiqun), and the second concerns the companions of the right. The second is that abrogation (naskh) in reports is not permissible, so when Allah, exalted is He, informs about them as few, it is not permissible for Him to inform about them as many in that respect. What he mentioned about the impermissibility of abrogation in reports, i.e. in their content absolutely, is the preferred view.

It has been said: abrogation is permissible in what changes, if it concerns the future, because Allah may erase what He decrees, and the report follows it. This is the view of al-Baydawi. It has been said: it is permissible also concerning the past, and this is the view of Imam al-Razi and al-Amidi. As for the abrogation of the content of a report when it is something that does not change, such as the existence of the Creator and the createdness of the world, it is impermissible by consensus. If what we are dealing with is something that changes, then its abrogation is permissible according to al-Baydawi, and the apparent meaning of the second report of Abu Hurayrah agrees with him. It is not permissible according to the preferred view held by al-Shafi'i and others. So the statement of the author of al-Kashf: "There is no disagreement about the impermissibility of abrogation in a report like what has been mentioned, since it does not contain a legal ruling that is free of something" [is not clear].

I say: what al-Zamakhshari mentioned may be challenged by the fact that the hadith is authentic (sahih), and that the first verse's being revealed concerning the foremost and the second concerning the companions of the right does not negate its implication. For it is permissible to say: when the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, heard the first verse, they supposed that the matter in this community would proceed along this course, so that the companions of the right would be a company of the earlier ones with only a few of them, and the successful ones to Paradise from the past nations would outnumber them. So they grieved over that, and then the saying of Allah, exalted is He, about the companions of the right was revealed: ﴿A company of the earlier ones﴾ and ﴿and a company of the later ones﴾, and the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, said to them what he said, by which their grief was removed. There is no abrogation of the report in this, as is not hidden.

As for the saying of Abu Hurayrah, "and it abrogated ﴿and few of the later ones﴾", if it is authentic from him, it should be interpreted as: he meant by it, "it removed the supposition that there would be mentioned of the successful ones to Paradise from this community, other than the foremost, anything like it. So reflect."

From Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her: the two groups, i.e. in His saying ﴿A company of the earlier ones﴾ and ﴿and few of the later ones﴾, are in the community of each prophet: at its beginning there is a company, and at its end there is a few. It has also been said: they are both from the prophets, upon them be peace; they were many at the beginning of the world and few at its end.

Abu Hayyan said:

*"It has come in the hadith: 'The two groups are in my community: the foremost of the beginning of the community is a company, and the foremost of the rest of it until the Day of Resurrection is few.'"*

The end of his words. Something similar has come concerning the two groups of the companions of the right. Musaddad in his Musnad, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated with a good chain (sanad hasan) from Abu Bakrah, may Allah be pleased with him, "from the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, concerning His saying, glorified is He: ﴿A company of the earlier ones﴾ and ﴿and a company of the later ones﴾, he said: 'They are both together from this community.'"

A group also narrated with a weak chain (sanad da'if) from Ibn Abbas, raised to the Prophet, with the wording: "They are both together from my community."

And according to this, the address in His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And you were three kinds of pairs﴾ is to this community alone.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 56, verses 13–14:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿A company of the earlier generations﴾ is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada', the subject of a nominal sentence), i.e. "they are a company," and so on. It is permitted that it be a subject whose predicate is omitted, i.e. "from among them," or that it be a first or second predicate, "for those" (li-ula'ika). Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a subject whose predicate is ﴿on thrones﴾. The thullah (company) in the commonly known usage is a group, whether large or small. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is a community of many people from among the people, and he cited his saying:

*"There came to them a thullah of the Khindif tribe, with an army like a torrent of flood-water, foaming."*

His saying after it: ﴿and few﴾ and so on is sufficient proof of the largeness (of the thullah). The end of his words. The apparent meaning is that he cited the verse as evidence for the meaning of abundance in thullah. If the ba' (in the poem's phrasing, "bi-jaysh") is taqridiyya (a ba' of emphasis that strips the meaning of an intensive sense), which is the apparent case, then the matter is explicit. Otherwise, the inference for it is that the context is one of hyperbole and praise. As for his inference from what follows, that is because contrast (taqabul) is required, since thullah was not established by consensus to mean "few," so that what follows should be taken as a limitation. Rather, it is either for abundance, and derivation from it is more indicative, because thall means pouring out and also complete demolition, while thullah with a kasra means a large flock of sheep. Or it is for a general sense of group, like firqah (faction) and qit'ah (portion), from thall meaning breaking, as if it were a group broken off and cut away from the people. However, usage has predominated for it to mean the large number. So the meaning is: a large group of the earlier ones, namely the people who went before from Adam until our Prophet, upon both of them and upon the great prophets between them be blessings and peace. ﴿And few of the later ones﴾: they are the people from our Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, until the Hour arises. This does not contradict his saying, upon him be blessings and peace:

"Indeed my community will outnumber the other nations." That is, they will surpass them in number. This is because the greater number of the forerunners among the earlier peoples compared with the forerunners of this community does not prevent the greater number of the followers of these from the followers of those.

The result of this is that the whole of this community surpasses others in number, like a village in which there are ten scholars and a hundred commoners, and another in which there are five scholars and a thousand commoners. The elite of the first are more numerous than the elite of the second, and the commoners of the second and the total of its people are many times those of the first. It may not be said that the greater number of the followers of these is contradicted by His saying: ﴿A company of the earlier ones﴾ and ﴿a company of the later ones﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 39, 40], since it refers to the companions of the right (ashab al-yamin), who are the followers, and He expressed each with thullah, i.e. a large group. This is because we say: there is no indication in the verse of more than the description of each of the two groups as numerous, and that does not contradict the greater number of one of them. Thus it results that the forerunners of the former nations are more numerous than the forerunners of our community, and the followers of our community are more numerous than the followers of the (other) nations. By "nations" is meant what includes the prophets, and then it is not far-fetched to say: the abundance of the forerunners of the earlier ones is only through their prophets, so there is no objection to the forerunners of this community, for most of them are forerunners of nations together with their prophets, upon them be peace.

Imam Ahmad, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "When there was revealed ﴿A company of the earlier ones﴾ and ﴿and few of the later ones﴾, that was hard upon the companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, so there was revealed ﴿A company of the earlier ones﴾ and ﴿and a company of the later ones﴾. Then the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, said: 'Indeed I hope that you will be a third of the people of Paradise; rather, you are half of the people of Paradise' (or 'a moiety of the people of Paradise'), 'and you will share the second half with them.'" The apparent meaning is that the fewness of those described by it was hard upon them, and that the second verse removed that, lifted it, and replaced it with abundance. What supports this is what Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "When there was revealed ﴿A company of the earlier ones﴾ and ﴿and few of the later ones﴾, the companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ grieved

[p. 135]

and said: 'Then there will be of the community of Muhammad ﷺ only a few.' So at midday there was revealed ﴿A company of the earlier ones﴾ and ﴿and a company of the later ones﴾, and it abrogated ﴿and few of the later ones﴾." Al-Zamakhshari rejected this and said: the report is not sound, for two reasons.

The first is that the first verse concerns the foremost (al-sabiqun), and the second concerns the companions of the right. The second is that abrogation (naskh) in reports is not permissible, so when Allah, exalted is He, informs about them as few, it is not permissible for Him to inform about them as many in that respect. What he mentioned about the impermissibility of abrogation in reports, i.e. in their content absolutely, is the preferred view.

It has been said: abrogation is permissible in what changes, if it concerns the future, because Allah may erase what He decrees, and the report follows it. This is the view of al-Baydawi. It has been said: it is permissible also concerning the past, and this is the view of Imam al-Razi and al-Amidi. As for the abrogation of the content of a report when it is something that does not change, such as the existence of the Creator and the createdness of the world, it is impermissible by consensus. If what we are dealing with is something that changes, then its abrogation is permissible according to al-Baydawi, and the apparent meaning of the second report of Abu Hurayrah agrees with him. It is not permissible according to the preferred view held by al-Shafi'i and others. So the statement of the author of al-Kashf: "There is no disagreement about the impermissibility of abrogation in a report like what has been mentioned, since it does not contain a legal ruling that is free of something" [is not clear].

I say: what al-Zamakhshari mentioned may be challenged by the fact that the hadith is authentic (sahih), and that the first verse's being revealed concerning the foremost and the second concerning the companions of the right does not negate its implication. For it is permissible to say: when the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, heard the first verse, they supposed that the matter in this community would proceed along this course, so that the companions of the right would be a company of the earlier ones with only a few of them, and the successful ones to Paradise from the past nations would outnumber them. So they grieved over that, and then the saying of Allah, exalted is He, about the companions of the right was revealed: ﴿A company of the earlier ones﴾ and ﴿and a company of the later ones﴾, and the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, said to them what he said, by which their grief was removed. There is no abrogation of the report in this, as is not hidden.

As for the saying of Abu Hurayrah, "and it abrogated ﴿and few of the later ones﴾", if it is authentic from him, it should be interpreted as: he meant by it, "it removed the supposition that there would be mentioned of the successful ones to Paradise from this community, other than the foremost, anything like it. So reflect."

From Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her: the two groups, i.e. in His saying ﴿A company of the earlier ones﴾ and ﴿and few of the later ones﴾, are in the community of each prophet: at its beginning there is a company, and at its end there is a few. It has also been said: they are both from the prophets, upon them be peace; they were many at the beginning of the world and few at its end.

Abu Hayyan said:

*"It has come in the hadith: 'The two groups are in my community: the foremost of the beginning of the community is a company, and the foremost of the rest of it until the Day of Resurrection is few.'"*

The end of his words. Something similar has come concerning the two groups of the companions of the right. Musaddad in his Musnad, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated with a good chain (sanad hasan) from Abu Bakrah, may Allah be pleased with him, "from the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, concerning His saying, glorified is He: ﴿A company of the earlier ones﴾ and ﴿and a company of the later ones﴾, he said: 'They are both together from this community.'"

A group also narrated with a weak chain (sanad da'if) from Ibn Abbas, raised to the Prophet, with the wording: "They are both together from my community."

And according to this, the address in His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And you were three kinds of pairs﴾ is to this community alone.

On thrones woven with gold (ﷺ no) — let me translate properly:

"On couches interwoven" — ﴿Reclining on couches woven together﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the foremost ones (al-Muqarrabūn), or to their pronoun in His saying, "in the Gardens of Bliss" (fī jannāt al-na'īm), based on the view that it occupies the position of a circumstantial clause, as was previously explained. It is also said that it is another predicate (khabar) for the deleted pronoun which is the subject of the predicate mentioned first, "a multitude" (bi-thullah). There is another possibility, to which we pointed earlier. And "mawḍūnah" (woven together) derives from al-waḍn, which is the weaving of a coat of mail. Al-A'shā said:

"And of the weaving of Dawud is a woven one, moving with the tribe, caravan after caravan."

The term is extended to general weaving, or to a particular tight weave. From this comes the waḍīn of the she-camel, which is her girth, because it is woven (mawḍūn), that is, twisted (maftūl). The meaning here, as reported by Ibn Jarir and others from Ibn 'Abbas, is "marmūlah," that is, woven with gold. In another narration from him, it means with silver rods. 'Ikrimah said: "interlaced with pearls and rubies." It is also said that "mawḍūnah" means that its parts are joined to one another like the rings of a coat of mail, and the meaning is that they are closely arranged.

Zayd ibn 'Ali and Abu al-Sammal read "surar" with a fatḥah on the rā', and this is a dialect of some of the Tamim and Kalb, who pronounce the 'ayn of the pattern fu'ul (the plural of the doubled fa'īl) such as "sarīr" with a fatḥah.

﴿Reclining upon them﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in the prepositional phrase "upon couches," and His saying, ﴿facing one another﴾, is also a circumstantial clause from it. You may consider the two circumstantial clauses as interlocking.

The meaning, as Mujahid said, is that none of them looks at the back of his companion. This is a description of them with good companionship, refinement of character, observance of etiquette, and purity of inner hearts.

وقَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿يَطُوفُ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ [they will be circulated among them] حالٌ أُخْرى أوِ اسْتِئْنافٌ [another circumstantial clause (ḥāl) or a resumptive clause (isti'nāf)]، أيْ يَدُورُ حَوْلَهم لِلْخِدْمَةِ ﴿وِلْدانٌ مُخَلَّدُونَ﴾ [youths made eternal]، أيْ مُبْقُونَ أبَدًا عَلى شَكْلِ الوِلْدانِ وحَدُّ الوَصّافَةِ [remaining forever in the form of youths and the bloom of youthful adolescence]، لا يَتَحَوَّلُونَ عَنْ ذَلِكَ، وإلّا فَكَلُّ أهْلِ الجَنَّةِ مُخَلَّدٌ لا يَمُوتُ، وقالَ الفَرّاءُ [al-Farrā'] وابْنُ جُبَيْرٍ [Ibn Jubayr]: مُقْرَطُونَ بِخِلَدَةٍ [adorned with earrings of khalda (a kind of earring)]، وهي ضَرْبٌ مِنَ الأقْراطِ قِيلَ:

هَمْ أوْلادُ أهْلِ الدُّنْيا لَمْ يَكُنْ لَهم حَسَناتٌ فَيُثابُوا عَلَيْها ولا سَيِّئاتٌ فَيُعاقِبُوا عَلَيْها، ورَوى هَذا أمِيرُ المُؤْمِنِينَ عَلِيٌّ كَرَّمَ اللَّهُ تَعالى وجْهَهُ [may God ennoble his face]، وعَنِ الحَسَنِ البَصْرِيِّ [al-Hasan al-Basri] -

واشْتُهِرَ أنَّهُ عَلَيْهِ الصَّلاةُ والسَّلامُ [upon him be blessings and peace] - قالَ: «أوْلادُ الكُفّارِ خَدَمُ أهْلِ الجَنَّةِ»

- وذَكَرَ الطَّيِّبِيُّ [al-Ṭībī] أنَّهُ لَمْ يَصِحْ بَلْ صَحَّ ما يَدْفَعُهُ:

أخْرَجَ البُخارِيُّ [al-Bukhārī] وأبُو داوُدَ [Abū Dāwūd] والنَّسائِيُّ [al-Nasā'ī] «عَنْ عائِشَةَ [ʿĀ'isha] قالَتْ: تُوُفِّيَ صَبِيٌّ فَقُلْتُ: طُوبى لَهُ عُصْفُورٌ في الجَنَّةِ فَقالَ صَلّى اللَّهُ تَعالى عَلَيْهِ وسَلَّمَ (ﷺ): أوْ لا تَدْرِينَ أنَّ اللَّهَ تَعالى خَلَقَ الجَنَّةَ وخَلَقَ النّارَ فَخَلَقَ لِهَذِهِ أهْلًا ولِهَذِهِ أهْلًا، وفي رِوايَةٍ خَلَقَهم لَها وهم في أصْلابِ آبائِهِمْ».

وأخْرَجَ أبُو داوُدَ عَنْها أنَّها قالَتْ: «قُلْتُ: يا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ ذَرارِيُّ المُؤْمِنِينَ فَقالَ مِن آبائِهِمْ فَقُلْتُ: يا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ بِلا عَمَلٍ قالَ: اللَّهُ أعْلَمُ بِما كانُوا عامِلِينَ قُلْتُ: يا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ فَذَرارِيُّ المُشْرِكِينَ قالَ: مِن آبائِهِمْ فَقُلْتُ: بِلا عَمَلٍ قالَ: اللَّهُ أعْلَمُ بِما كانُوا عامِلِينَ، وقِيلَ: إنَّهم يُمْتَحَنُونَ يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ فَتَخْرُجُ لَهم نارٌ ويُؤْمَرُونَ بِالدُّخُولِ فِيها فَمَن دَخَلَها وجَدَها بَرْدًا وسَلامًا وأُدْخِلَ الجَنَّةَ، ومَن أبى أُدْخِلَ النّارَ مَعَ سائِرِ الكُفّارِ» ويَرْوُونَ في ذَلِكَ أثَرًا.

ومِنَ الغَرِيبِ ما قِيلَ: إنَّهم بَعْدُ الإعادَةِ يَكُونُونَ تُرابًا كالبَهائِمِ، وفي الكَشْفِ [al-Kashf] الأحادِيثُ مُتَعارِضَةٌ في المَسْألَةِ وكَذَلِكَ المَذاهِبُ، والمَسْألَةُ ظَنِّيَّةُ والعِلْمُ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ تَعالى وهو عَزَّ وجَلَّ أعْلَمُ انْتَهى والأكْثَرُ عَلى دُخُولِهِمُ الجَنَّةَ بِفَضْلِ اللَّهِ تَعالى ومَزِيدِ رَحْمَتِهِ تَبارَكَ وتَعالى، وسَيَأْتِي إنْ شاءَ اللَّهُ تَعالى تَمامُ الكَلامِ في ذَلِكَ.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 56, verse 18:**

﴿with cups﴾: vessels that have neither handles nor spouts. The apparent meaning is that they are drinking-cups, and Ikrimah interpreted it this way. The word is the plural of *kub*.

﴿and jugs﴾: the plural of *ibriq* (ewer), a vessel with a spout. It is said that it also has a handle. Al-Bahr (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) states that it is among the vessels used for wine. He cited the verse of 'Adi ibn Zayd:

*"They called for the morning draught one day, and there came a serving-girl with an ewer in her right hand."*

Also in al-Bahr, it is said that *ibriq* is a pattern (*if'il*) derived from *buruq* (gleam). Many scholars have said that it is a *mu'arrab* (a loanword Arabicized from another language), from *ab rizay* (water-pourer). This is more suitable than what is found in some copies of al-Qamus, that it is *mu'arrab* from *ab ri* without a *zay*. Whatever the case, it is not derived from *buruq*. Yet *ibriq* in the sense of a beautiful woman, a shining woman, a gleaming sword, or a bow with streaks in it is derived from that root. Perhaps the author holds that it is Arabic and not a loanword, and that *buruq* refers to the wine, which the poets describe with it, as in his saying:

*"Sparkling, as if the gypsum in it, when water mixes with it while it is hot..."*

Or because it is generally made of something that has a kind of gleam, such as crystal or silver.

﴿and a cup from a flowing spring﴾: that is, wine flowing from the springs, as Ibn Abbas and Qatadah said, meaning it has not been pressed, unlike the wine of this world. It is also said: it is wine that is visible to the eyes, seen through them, because it is more wholesome in that state. The word *ka's* (cup) is in the singular, according to what is said, because it is not called a *ka's* unless it is full.

[Page 137]

﴿They will not be afflicted with headache from it﴾, meaning: because of it, and its true sense. Their headache does not arise from it. The intended meaning is that no headache reaches their heads on account of an intoxication that results from it, as happens with the wines of this world. It is also said: "they will not be separated from it," meaning their pleasure will not be cut off from them by any cause, as the people of worldly wine are separated from it in various ways.

Mujahid recited «لا يَصَّدَّعُونَ» with a fatha on the yā' and a shaddah on the ṣād, on the basis that the original form is yatasaddaʿūn, and the tā' was assimilated into the ṣād (idgham, the merging of one consonant into the next). The meaning is "they will not disperse," like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On that Day they will be separated﴾ [al-Rum: 43]. It has also been read «لا يَصْدَعُونَ» with a fatha on the yā' and without the shaddah, meaning: none of them will cause another to have a headache, nor will they separate them. That is, one of them does not sit between two people and thereby separate those who are close to one another, for that is bad manners and is not among the good conduct of companionship. ﴿Nor will they be made drunk﴾. Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: their minds will not be taken away by its intoxication, from the verb nazafa (to be drained), as in ʿaniya, when the drinker's reason departs. The intoxicated person is called nazīf and manzūf. It is also said that it derives from nazafa al-māʾ, meaning he drew water from the well little by little. In that case the statement is elliptical, with an omitted noun (muḍāf, a construction in which a word is understood by implication).

Ibn Abi Ishaq, ʿAbd Allah, al-Sulami, al-Jahdari, al-Aʿmash, Talhah, ʿIsa and ʿAsim, as transmitted from him by ʿAbd ibn Humayd, recited «وَلَا يُنْزِفُونَ» with a ḍammah on the yā' and a kasrah on the zāy, from anzafa al-sharib, when the drinker's reason or his drink is exhausted. Its meaning is that he becomes one who is drained, and its parallel is aqshaʿa al-sarab (the mirage vanished) and qashaʿathu al-rīḥ (the wind dispersed it); its real sense is that he entered into the state of being dispersed. Ibn Abi Ishaq also recited «وَلَا يَنْزِفُونُ» with a fatha on the yā' and a kasrah on the zāy. Al-Majmaʿ (Majmaʿ al-Bayan, the commentary of al-Tabarsi) said: this is understood to mean that their wine never runs out. The relationship between the two clauses, as you have heard in the first place, according to the reading of the majority, is that the first clause explains the negation of harm to the bodies, and the second explains the negation of harm to the intellects. Reflect on this so that you may come to understand what lies beyond it, God willing, Exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 56, verse 20–21:

﴿And fruit from whatever they choose﴾, meaning: they take the best and finest of it, and what is intended is what they are pleased with. ﴿And the flesh of fowl from whatever they desire﴾, meaning: from what their souls incline to and long for. The apparent view is that "fruit" and "flesh of fowl" are conjoined to "cups", so the verse conveys that the youths circulate with these among them. It has been raised as an objection that reports have come that the fruit of Paradise and its produce can be reached by one who is standing, sitting, or lying down. It is also reported from Mujahid that the fruit is brought near to its owners, so they take it while reclining; when they lie down, it descends in front of their mouths, so they take it while lying down. And that a man of the people of Paradise desires a bird from the birds of Paradise, and it falls into his hand roasted and cooked. Ibn Abi al-Dunya reported this from Abu Umamah.

And he reported from Maymunah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "A man in Paradise desires a bird, and it comes like a Bukhti camel until it lands upon his platter; it has not been touched by smoke nor has fire touched it. He eats from it until he is satisfied, then it flies off to elsewhere." If the matter is as mentioned, then the circulating of them with fruit and flesh is unnecessary. It is answered that this, and Allah the Exalted knows best, is the state of gathering and drinking, and they do this for honour, increased love, glorification and respect. This is like one of the companions at a table passing to another some of the fruits and the like that are upon it, even though it is near him, out of care for his standing, showing his love and honouring him. It is also permitted that the conjunction is to "gardens of delight," and that is of the type of "wearing a sword and a spear", or of its well-known type. The placing of fruit before flesh is to indicate that they are not in a state that calls for giving precedence to meat, as with the hungry, for his need for meat is greater than his need for fruit. Rather, they are in a state that calls for giving precedence to fruit and choosing it, as with the satiated, for he inclines to fruit more than to meat. It is also permitted that this is because the custom of the people of this world, especially their drinkers, is to put fruit first in eating, and this is medically recommended, for it is lighter, passes down more quickly, and needs less time to remain in the stomach for digestion. They have mentioned that one of the causes of indigestion is putting something light of food upon something heavy, and because fruit stirs the appetite for eating, while meat generally suppresses it.

From the first aspect, the reason is known for restricting "choosing" to fruit and "desiring" to flesh, and in it there is an indication that fruit remains present with them and before their eyes, unlike meat; the reason for that is that it is what the eyes delight in, unlike it. It has been said: the reason for the restriction is the great variety of fruits, their differing tastes, colours and shapes, and that meat is not like that. In the expression "yatakhayyarun" rather than "yakhtarun", though they are close in meaning, there is an indication, because of the form of the tafa''ala pattern, that they take from it what is in the utmost perfection, and that they are in the utmost independence from it. And Allah the Exalted knows best the secrets of His speech.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 56, verse 20–21:

﴿And fruit from whatever they choose﴾, meaning: they take the best and finest of it, and what is intended is what they are pleased with. ﴿And the flesh of fowl from whatever they desire﴾, meaning: from what their souls incline to and long for. The apparent view is that "fruit" and "flesh of fowl" are conjoined to "cups", so the verse conveys that the youths circulate with these among them. It has been raised as an objection that reports have come that the fruit of Paradise and its produce can be reached by one who is standing, sitting, or lying down. It is also reported from Mujahid that the fruit is brought near to its owners, so they take it while reclining; when they lie down, it descends in front of their mouths, so they take it while lying down. And that a man of the people of Paradise desires a bird from the birds of Paradise, and it falls into his hand roasted and cooked. Ibn Abi al-Dunya reported this from Abu Umamah.

And he reported from Maymunah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "A man in Paradise desires a bird, and it comes like a Bukhti camel until it lands upon his platter; it has not been touched by smoke nor has fire touched it. He eats from it until he is satisfied, then it flies off to elsewhere." If the matter is as mentioned, then the circulating of them with fruit and flesh is unnecessary. It is answered that this, and Allah the Exalted knows best, is the state of gathering and drinking, and they do this for honour, increased love, glorification and respect. This is like one of the companions at a table passing to another some of the fruits and the like that are upon it, even though it is near him, out of care for his standing, showing his love and honouring him. It is also permitted that the conjunction is to "gardens of delight," and that is of the type of "wearing a sword and a spear", or of its well-known type. The placing of fruit before flesh is to indicate that they are not in a state that calls for giving precedence to meat, as with the hungry, for his need for meat is greater than his need for fruit. Rather, they are in a state that calls for giving precedence to fruit and choosing it, as with the satiated, for he inclines to fruit more than to meat. ﴿And [there are] houris, with wide, lovely eyes﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) either with *wildan* (youths), or with the hidden pronoun in *muttaki'īn* (reclining), or with a subject whose subject and predicate have both been omitted, meaning: "for them is this, all of it, and houris." Alternatively, *ḥūrun* is a subject whose predicate has been omitted, meaning "for them," or "in it there are houris." The first possibility has been objected to on the ground that circulating [with the cups] does not suit the state of the houris. The reply is that it is not far-fetched for some houris to be those who are not kept secluded in tents or veiled, but are like servants to them, whose circulating is not objected to and who are not reprimanded for it. It is also said that the circulating takes place within the tents themselves, and this does not contradict their being kept secluded in them. Or the coordination is with the meaning of *lahum* ("for them"), so that it reads: *wildānun wa ḥūrun* ("youths and houris"). The second possibility is said to be highly contrary to the apparent sense, and the third to involve excessive omission.

*ʿīnun* is the plural of *ʿaynāʾ* (wide-eyed, feminine). Its original form is *ʿuynun* on the pattern *fuʿlun*, as one says *ḥamrāʾ* and *ḥumrun*. The *ʿayn* was then given a kasra so that the *yāʾ* would not be changed into a *wāw*. In the speech of the Arabs there is no sukūn-*yāʾ* preceded by a ḍamma, just as there is no sukūn-*wāw* preceded by a kasra.

al-Sulamī, al-Ḥasan, ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd, Abū Jaʿfar, Shayba, al-Aʿmash, Ṭalḥa, al-Mufaddal, Abān, and ʿIṣma from ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read ﴿وحُورٍ عِينٍ﴾ with a kasra on the final letters (*ḥūrin ʿīnin*). al-Nakhaʿī read it likewise, except that he changed the *wāw* of *ḥūrin* into a *yāʾ* and the ḍamma before it into a kasra, saying *ḥīrin* by way of assimilation (ittibāʿ) to *ʿīnin*. This reading is interpreted as coordination with *jannāti al-naʿīm* ("Gardens of Bliss"), with an omitted genitive (muḍāf), as if it were said: "they are in gardens, and fruit, and meat, and in the company of houris." The company of houris is treated as a container (ẓarf) by way of an implicit metaphor (istiʿāra makniyya), whose indicator (qarīna) is the imaginative indicator (takhyīliyya), namely the affirmation of the meaning of containment through the word *fī* ("in"). Thus *fī* remains on its literal meaning, and there is no combining of the literal and the figurative. al-Zamakhsharī went to this coordination, and Abū Ḥayyān objected to it, saying: "It is remote, and it separates speech that is connected, one part to another, and it is a non-Arabic understanding." This is not as he said, as is not hidden. Or it is coordinated with *akwāb* ("cups"), and it is considered of the type of "wearing a sword and a spear" (*mutaqqilidan sayfan wa rumḥan*), as you have heard just now. So it is as if it were said: "they are given delight with cups and with houris." It is also permitted that it remains on its well-known apparent sense, and that the youths also circulate among them with the houris, to present the kinds of pleasures to them, of food, drink, and intercourse, just as servants bring concubines to kings and present them. This was the view of Abū ʿAmr and Quṭrub. The author of al-Kashf rejected this, saying: "As for coordination with the youths on the apparent sense, no, because the youths do not circulate with them in the way they circulate with the cups. The inclination is toward this, unless there is some evidence indicating otherwise. And that the *jarr* is by proximity (jiwār) is refuted by the intervening word (faṣl), or it weakens it."

Ubayy and ʿAbd Allāh read ﴿وحُورًا عِينًا﴾ with a fatḥa (*ḥūran ʿīnan*). This is interpreted as coordination with the grammatical location (maḥall) of ﴿بِأكْوابٍ﴾ ("with cups"), since the meaning is "they are given cups and houris," with *ḥūran* as the direct object of an omitted verb, meaning "and they are given houris." Or it is coordinated with an omitted object that was itself the direct object of an omitted verb, meaning "they are given all this, and houris."

Qatāda read *ḥūru* with a ḍamma, in construct with *ʿīnin*. Ibn Muqsim read *ḥūra* with a fatḥa, in construct. ʿIkrima read *wa-ḥawrāʾa ʿaynāʾa* with the singular, as a collective noun (ism jins), and with a fatḥa on the hamza in both words, so that it admits both the genitive and the accusative.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 56, verse 23–24:

﴿As the likeness of hidden pearls﴾ meaning in their purity. It is qualified by "hidden," i.e., concealed by that which protects it, because it is purer and further from change. In a hadith, "Their purity is like the purity of the pearl that no hands have touched." Describing beautiful women by this is common among the Arabs, and from it is the saying of the poet:

She stood, appearing between two curtains of a veil,
like the sun on the day of its rising, in the brightest of lights.

Page 139
Or a pearl of the oyster, whose diver ∗∗∗ is joyful; whenever he sees it, he exclaims (Allahu akbar) and prostrates.

The prepositional phrase (al-jarr wa'l-majrur) is in the position of a qualifier (sifah) for "houris," or of a circumstantial phrase (hal). The use of the particle "ka" (like) is for emphasis in the comparison, and perhaps the matter is as in the expression "Zayd is a moon." ﴿A reward for what they used to do﴾ is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) for a verb omitted, meaning: all of that is done to them as a reward for their deeds, or for what they continued to practise; or it is an emphatic verbal noun (masdar muakkid), meaning: they are rewarded with a reward.

﴿They hear therein no idle talk﴾: what is not counted as speech, namely that which is uttered without deliberation or thought, so it goes in the manner of *al-laghā* (idle chatter), which is the sound of sparrows and similar birds. Every ugly speech may also be called *laghw* (idle talk). ﴿Nor any sinfulness﴾: that is, nor any attribution to sin, meaning it is not said to them, "You have sinned."

It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, as Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded, that he explained it as lying. Hannād also narrated it from al-Ḍaḥḥāk. This is metaphorical, as is not hidden. The speech here is in the pattern of "and you do not see the lizard burrowing therein" (*wa-lā tarā al-ḍabba bihā yanjaḥiru*).

﴿except the saying﴾: that is, *qawlan*, so it is a verbal noun of the same kind. ﴿"Peace, peace"﴾ (*salāman salāman*) is a *badal* (substitute) for *qīlā*, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They hear therein no idle talk, except "Peace."﴾ [Maryam: 62]

Al-Zajjāj said: it is an adjective for it, by interpreting it as a derivative, meaning "safe from these defects," or it is its object (*maf'ūl*), and what is meant is its wording, which is why it may be the object of the saying despite being in the singular. The meaning is: "except that some of them say to others '*Salāman*.'" It was also said: it is a verbal noun of an implied verb derived from its wording, and it is then the object of the saying, meaning "we greet with a greeting." The repetition indicates the spread and abundance of greeting among them, since what is meant is greeting after greeting.

The exception is *munqaṭiʿ* (disjunct). It belongs to the type of emphasizing praise by means resembling dispraise (*taʾkīd al-madḥ bi-mā yushbihu al-dhamm*). It may be of the first type of this, which is that one excepts from a negated attribute of dispraise a praise attribute of the thing, on the assumption that it falls within what was negated, so that peace is taken here as included in what is said, giving emphasis from two angles. Or it may be of the second type, which is that one affirms a praise attribute for a thing and follows it with an exceptive particle followed by another praise attribute, without assuming that inclusion, and makes the exception disjunct from its origin, giving emphasis from one angle.

Were it not for the mention of *taʾthīm* (attributing sin), according to what al-Saʿd said, it would be permissible to make the exception *muttaṣil* (contiguous) in reality. This is because the meaning of *salām* is a supplication for safety, and the people of Paradise have no need of that, so its outward sense would be of the kind of idle talk and superfluous speech, were it not for the benefit of honour in it. *Taʾthīm*, which is attributing sin, is prohibited because it is not possible to make greeting of its kind. It is not permissible in speech to mention several items and then bring a contiguous exception from the first, as when you say: "No man or woman came except Zayd." If you intended that, it would be necessary to postpone mention of the man.

It is also read *salāmun salāmun* with the nominative, as a quotation (*ḥikāya*).

**[Page 140]**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the companions of the right﴾, and so on, begins an account of the details of their condition after the account of the details of the foremost. "And the companions" is the subject (mubtada'). His saying: ﴿what are the companions of the right?﴾ is an interrogative clause that conveys their exaltation and the wonder at their state. According to what they have said, it is either the predicate (khabar) of the subject. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿among lote trees without thorns﴾ is a second predicate of it, or the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "they are among lote trees." The clause is a resumption (isti'naf) to explain what was left vague in His saying, mighty and majestic is He: "what are the companions of the right," regarding their loftiness of rank. Or it is a parenthetical clause (mu'taridah), and the predicate is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿among lote trees﴾.

It has also been permitted that this clause be in the position of a qualifier (sifah), and the predicate is this prepositional phrase. The clause is coordinated with His saying, blessed and exalted is He, in describing the condition of the foremost: ﴿Those are the ones brought near﴾ ﴿in the Gardens of Bliss﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 11, 12]. That is: ﴿and the companions of the right﴾, concerning whom it is said what the companions of the right are, are ﴿among lote trees﴾, and so on. The apparent view is that the expression "right side" (al-maymanah) was used above, and "the right" (al-yamin) here is for variety of expression (tafannun). The same applies to "left side" (al-mash'amah) and "left" (al-shimal) below. Al-Imam (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi) said: the wisdom in this is that in the right side, and likewise the left side, there is an indication of the place, and the three pairs at the outset are distinguished from one another, and they are separated by place. Therefore, the term that indicates the place is used first. Later, the distinction and separation are by a matter in them, so that term is not used a second time.

The lote tree (al-sidr) is the jujube tree (shajar al-nabq). "Makhdud" is that whose thorns have been cut off (khudida), i.e., its thorns have been cut. Al-Hakim transmitted it and declared it sound, and al-Bayhaqi transmitted it, from Abu Umamah, who said: "The companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to say: Allah, exalted is He, benefits us through the Bedouins and their questions. One day a Bedouin came and said: O Messenger of Allah, Allah, exalted is He, has mentioned in the Qur'an a harmful tree, and I did not think that there is in Paradise a tree that harms its companion. He said: And what is it? He said: The lote tree, for it has thorns. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: Does not Allah say: ﴿among lote trees without thorns﴾? Allah has cut off its thorns, and in place of every thorn He has made a fruit, and the fruit of it bursts open into seventy-two kinds of food, no two of which resemble one another."

Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, Ikrimah and al-Dahhak that "makhdud" means "laden with fruit" (al-muqawwar hilan), based on the sense of "khadd al-ghusn," i.e., bending the branch while it is fresh. So "makhdud" means one whose branches are bent, and it is a metaphor for abundant fruit.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Yazid al-Raqqashi that a single jujube was larger than large jars (qilal). The adverbial "in" (fi) here is metaphorical, for emphasis on their being fully enabled to enjoy luxury and to benefit from what has been mentioned.

﴿and talh trees, arranged in layers﴾: its fruit has been arranged (nudida) from its base to its top, and it has no visible trunk. It is the banana tree, as Abd al-Razzaq, Hannad, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face. A group transmitted it through several chains from Ibn Abbas. Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted it from Abu Hurayrah and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, and Abd ibn Humayd transmitted it from al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatadah. From al-Hasan, he said: "It is not the banana, but it is a tree whose shade is cool and moist." Al-Suddi said: "A tree resembling the talh of this world, but it has a fruit sweeter than honey." It was said: it is a tree among the large 'idah (thorny shrubs). It was said: it is the tree of Umm Ghaylan, which has abundant and fragrant blossoms.

﴿and extended shade﴾: spread out, extended, not contracting and not varying, like the shade between the break of dawn and sunrise. The apparent reports indicate that it is the shade of trees.

Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah and others transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "In Paradise there is a tree in whose shade a rider could travel for a hundred years without crossing it. Recite if you wish: ﴿and extended shade﴾."

Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Sa'id, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: In Paradise there is a tree in whose shade a rider could travel for a hundred years without crossing it, and that is the extended shade."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, who said: "The extended shade is a tree in Paradise on a single trunk, whose shade is such that a rider could travel through all its regions for a hundred years. The people of Paradise, the people of the chambers and others, go out to it and talk in its shade. Some of them desire, and mention the amusements of the world, and Allah, exalted is He, sends a wind from Paradise which moves that tree with every amusement of the world." And from Mujahid, who said: "This shade is from its lote trees and its talh trees." Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Amr ibn Maymun that he said: "The extended shade is a distance of seventy thousand years."

﴿and flowing water﴾: Sufyan and others said: flowing without trenches. It was said: spilling wherever they wish, without needing any water-wheel (saniyah) or rope (risha'). These things were mentioned because many believers, due to their being Bedouins, had wished for them. Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Mujahid, who said: "They used to admire Wajj and its shades of talh and lote trees, so Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿And the companions of the right, what are the companions of the right?﴾ ﴿among lote trees without thorns﴾, and so on." In another report from al-Dahhak: "The Muslims looked at Wajj, and its lote trees impressed them, and they said: O would that we had the like of this. So this verse was revealed."

**[Page 141]**

It has been said: when He likened the condition of the foremost to the highest thing that can be imagined for city dwellers, namely that they are on couches with their servants attending them with various delights, He likened the condition of the companions of the right to the most perfect thing that can be imagined for desert dwellers, namely their settling in fertile places with water, trees and shades. This signals that the difference between the two groups is like the difference between city dwellers and desert dwellers. Al-Imam mentioned, claiming that it was among what he was granted success in, that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿among lote trees without thorns﴾ and ﴿and talh trees arranged in layers﴾ is of the same type as His saying, glorified is He: "Lord of the East and the West" [ash-Shu'ara': 28; al-Muzzammil: 9]. This is because the leaves of the lote tree are very small, and the talh, meaning the banana, has very large leaves. Thus the reference falls on the two extremes, and all trees are intended, since in regard to their leaves they are confined between them. This is not objectionable.

Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, Ja'far ibn Muhammad and Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with them, read "wa-talh" with the letter ayn (ṭal'in, "spathes") instead of "wa-ṭalh" with the letter ha'. Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Qays ibn Abbad, who said: "I recited to Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, ﴿and talh trees arranged in layers﴾, and he said: What is the matter with talh? Do you not recite 'wa-ṭal'in'?" Then he recited His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for it are spathes piled one upon another﴾ [Qaf: 10]. Someone said to him: O Commander of the Faithful, shall we erase it from the Mushaf? He said: The Qur'an is not to be stirred up today. This report is not sound, as al-Tibi pointed out. How could the Commander of the Faithful, may Allah ennoble his face, approve of an alteration in the Book of Allah that is circulated among people? Or how could it be supposed that the transmitters, narrators and scribes of the Qur'an before him deliberately did that or were heedless of it? Allah, exalted is He, has undertaken its preservation. Glory be to You, this is a tremendous slander.

Then, what the sublime arrangement requires, as al-Tibi said, is to understand ﴿among lote trees without thorns﴾ and so on in the sense of shading and the density of trees, in an ascending manner, since the fruits are dispensed with by what follows, and so that it may correspond to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the companions of the left, what are the companions of the left?﴾ ﴿in scorching wind and boiling water﴾ ﴿and shade of black smoke﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 41–43]. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And the companions of the right﴾, and so on, is its counterpart. Accordingly, the narration about the spathes has no place in the meaning of shade and what is connected with it. However, the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: the description of talh as "arranged in layers" does not appear to fit well with the intended benefit of shading, and it is proper to understand talh as a large 'idah shrub, as he mentioned in al-Sihah (the lexicon of al-Jawhari). The tree of Umm Ghaylan and the banana have no shade worth considering. Then he said: "If talh were understood as the fragrant one, it would be a valid view." We have already set out for you the report of the occasion of revelation, so do not be heedless.

**[Page 141]**

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 56, verses 35–36:

The meaning of the women is supported by His the Exalted's words: ﴿Indeed, We created them with a special creation﴾, because the pronoun in most cases refers back to a previously mentioned noun, and the only one mentioned is the couches (*furush*). Referring it to them fits only on this meaning, and *istikhdam* (a rhetorical device in which one word is used in two senses, here the couches and the women) is far-fetched here. According to the view that the pronoun refers to the couches, the pronoun refers to the women even though they have not been mentioned, because something that indicates them has already come before. So it is a *tatmim* (a completing addition that supplies clarity) explaining an implied element that the context indicates, as if it were said: "And raised couches, and women, or the maidens of paradise (*hur 'in*)." Then their description is resumed with His, glory be to Him, words: ﴿Indeed, We created them﴾, as a *tatmim* of the explanation, to add encouragement, not to give the reason for the raising. It was also said that the referent is implied, and the sense is: "And raised couches for their husbands," or "for their wives, for indeed We created them," so that the clause is a *isti'naf* (a new sentence) giving the reason for the raising, meaning: "and raised couches for their husbands, because We created them." The first view is more fitting to the eloquence of the Mighty Qur'an. The meaning of "We created them" is "We renewed their creation without birth," because those spoken of in this way are your women in the world.

Ibn Jarir, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi and others related from Anas, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said about the verse: "Indeed, those who were created are the women who were in the world, old women, blear-eyed, with discharge in their eyes." Al-Tabarani, Ibn Abi Hatim and a group related from Salama ibn Marthad al-Ju'fi, who said: "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say about His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿Indeed, We created them with a special creation﴾: 'The married women and the virgins who were in the world.'" Al-Tirmidhi in al-Shama'il, Ibn al-Mundhir and others related from al-Hasan, who said: "An old woman came and said: 'O Messenger of God, pray to God that He admit me to paradise.' He said: 'O mother of so-and-so, indeed an old woman will not enter paradise.' She turned away weeping. He said: 'Tell her that she will not enter it while she is old, for indeed God, the Exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, We created them with a special creation﴾ etc.'"

Abu Hayyan said: The apparent meaning is that *insha'* (creation) is *ikhtira'* (bringing into being) that was not preceded by any creation, and that this applies specifically to the maidens of paradise. So the meaning is: "Indeed, We began them with a new beginning, without birth and without a prior creation." ﴿So We made them virgins﴾ is an explanation of what came before. The verb *ja'l* (making) may mean *taṣyīr* (rendering), in which case "virgins" (*abkaran*) is a second object, or it may mean *khalq* (creating), in which case "virgins" is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) or a second object. The speech is of the kind of "the narrowness of the mouth of the well," meaning concise and elliptical.

In a hadith, "Indeed, the people of paradise, when they have intercourse with their wives, return as virgins." Al-Tabarani in al-Saghir and al-Bazzar related it from Abu Sa'id, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 56, verse 37–38:

﴿ʿUruban﴾ (loving their husbands, amorous): the plural of ʿarub, like ṣabur and ṣubur. This is related from a group of the early generation (salaf), and another group explained it as "coquettish" (ghanijat). It is not hidden that coquetry (al-ghanaj) is the subtlest of the means of love. From Zayd ibn Aslam: al-ʿurub are those who are good in speech. In another report from Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid: they are those who are passionate (ʿawashiq) for their husbands. From this, as it is said, is the verse of Labid:

"And in the curtained chambers are ʿurub, not lewd, with full hips, whom the eye cannot reach beyond."

In another report from Mujahid: they are the youthful ones (al-ghulamat) who desire their husbands. Ibn ʿAdi related with a weak chain from Anas, marfu': "The best of your women is the chaste one who is ardent (al-ghulmah)." Ishaq ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Harith al-Nawfali said: al-ʿurub are the modest ones who are unrestrained (mutabadhdhilah) toward their husbands, and he recited:

"They are amorous with their husbands when they are alone, and when they go out, they are guardians (khifar)."

This returns to the sense of loving. Ibn Abi Hatim related from Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad, from his father, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said concerning His words, Exalted is He, ﴿ʿUruban﴾: their speech is Arabic." I do not think this has any authenticity. The explanation as "loving" is what most scholars hold.

Many said: it is for lightening, as in ʿunuq and ʿunq. ﴿Atraban﴾: equal in age, as Anas, Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah
