Al-Tirmidhi related from Mu'adh, marfu': "The people of Paradise will enter Paradise beardless, smooth-skinned, with kohl-darkened eyes, the age of thirty or thirty-three." What is meant by this is the perfection of youth.

His words, Exalted is He, ﴿li-ashab al-yamin﴾ (for the companions of the right hand): it is connected either to "anshanaha" (We created them) or to "ja'alna" (We made them). Hamzah and a group — among them ʿAbbas and al-Asmaʿi — transmitted from Abu ʿAmr; another group — among them Kharijah and Kardam — from Nafiʿ; and another group — among them Hammad, Abu Bakr and Aban — from ʿAsim, read "ʿurban" with the letter ra' vowelless (sukun), and this is the dialect of Tamim. Many said: it is for lightening, as in ʿunuq and ʿunq. ﴿Atraban﴾: equal in age, as Anas, Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah
صفحة 143
and Qatadah and others said. It is as if they were likened in equality to the tara'ib, which are the ribs of the chest; or as if they fell together upon the dust, i.e. the earth, and they are daughters of thirty-three years, and likewise their husbands.

Al-Tirmidhi related from Mu'adh, marfu': "The people of Paradise will enter Paradise beardless, smooth-skinned, with kohl-darkened eyes, the age of thirty or thirty-three." What is meant by this is the perfection of youth.

His words, Exalted is He, ﴿li-ashab al-yamin﴾ (for the companions of the right hand): it is connected either to "anshanaha" (We created them) or to "ja'alna" (We made them). It was also said: it is connected to "atraban" as in your saying "fulan turb li-fulan," meaning equal to him; but this requires interpretation (ta'wil), and it was objected that even so there is not much benefit in it, though this is open to question. It was also said: it is connected to an omitted word which is a description of "abkaran," i.e. they are existing for the companions of the right hand; and in this is the placing of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun, due to the length of time or for emphasis and confirmation. [al-Waqi'ah: 39–80].

The Exalted's words: ﴿A multitude from the earlier peoples﴾ ﴿and a multitude from the later ones﴾ are a predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), meaning: they are a multitude. Or they are a second predicate of "them" (lahum), with the predicate (muqaddar) being mubtada' together with ﴿in lote-trees without thorns﴾, or ﴿for the companions of the right﴾ in His words: ﴿And the companions of the right, what of the companions of the right?﴾. Or it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, meaning: from among them. Or it is a subject whose predicate is the prepositional phrase (al-jar wa al-majrur) before it. These are possibilities, and the last of them has been objected to on the grounds that the meaning under it is not apparent and has no elegance. Taking the lam to mean "min" (from), as in the line: "And we, for you, on the Day of Resurrection, are the best," is also of doubtful standing.

As for "the earlier ones and the later ones" (al-awwalun wa al-akhirun), they mean those who came before and those who came after, either from the nations in general and this nation, or from this nation alone, as you have heard in what preceded.

Furthermore, the Glorified did not say concerning the companions of the right "as a recompense for what they used to do," as He, Mighty and Majestic, said concerning the foremost (al-sabiqun). This is a sign that their excellence is purely a matter of favour, as though their deeds, because of their deficiency compared to the deeds of the foremost, were not taken into account.

Then, the apparent meaning is that what has been mentioned of the state of the companions of the right is the state in which they end up. Therefore it does not contradict that some of them may be punished for sins they committed and died without repenting of, and then they enter Paradise.

It cannot be said that the believing sinner is among the companions of the left, because the explicit description of them that follows requires that they were disbelievers. And making this a separate category would entail that the division is not exhaustive, so let this be considered. And God Most High knows best.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 56, verses 41–44:

The discussion of His saying, ﴿And the companions of the left hand—what are the companions of the left hand?﴾ ﴿In scorching wind and boiling water﴾, follows the same pattern as what has preceded in its counterpart. As for al-Samum (scorching wind), al-Raghib said: it is the hot wind that acts like poison (summ). In al-Kashshaf: it is the heat of a fire that penetrates the pores. The tanwin (nunation) here is for magnification, and likewise in His saying, ﴿and boiling water﴾, which is water of intense heat, ﴿and a shade of black smoke﴾, that is, black smoke, as said by Ibn Abbas, Abu Malik, Ibn Zayd and the majority. It is on the pattern of yafu'ul, and it has few parallels. Al-Humumah is a piece of charcoal. Calling it ﴿shade﴾ is by way of sarcastic likeness (al-tashbih al-tahakkumi). It is also reported from Ibn Abbas that it is the enclosing canopy (suradiq) of the Fire that surrounds its people, rising from every side until it shades them. Ibn Kaysan said: it is one of the names of Jahannam, for it is black, and everything in it is black and dark; we seek refuge in Allah from it. Ibn Buraydah and Ibn Zayd also said: it is a black mountain of fire to which the people of the Fire flee for refuge, only to find it the most severe of things. The prepositional phrase (al-jar wa al-majrur) is in the position of an attribute to "shade." Likewise His saying, glorified is He, ﴿neither cool nor generous﴾ are two attributes of it. Placing the prepositional-phrase attribute before the single-word attribute is permissible, as al-Radi and others have stated. That is: not cool like other shades, nor beneficial to one who takes refuge in it from the harm of the heat; and that is its generosity. So here there is a metaphor (isti'arah). The negation is to eliminate any assumption of the relief one might find in shade, even though it was first described by His saying, ﴿of black smoke﴾. The meaning is that it is a shade that is hot and harmful, but negation has an effect that affirmation does not. From this comes the sarcasm and allusion that the one deserving the shade in which there is coolness and honor is other than these, so that it would be more grievous to their throats and more intense for their regret. It was also said: "generous" is considered in terms of it being praiseworthy in its kind; so the generous shade is the one praised for its coolness and refreshment. But this objection stands: it does not fit here, given His saying, ﴿neither cool﴾. It is also permitted that this is a negation of the honor of one who finds relief in it, and it is attributed to the shade metaphorically; the meaning being that they shade themselves with it while they are humiliated. It may also imply a bad seat for gaining honor. In al-Bahr: it is permissible that both be attributes of "yahmum," which would entail describing the shade with them. It was objected that describing yahmum, which is smoke, with this has no great benefit. Ibn Abi Abla read "la barid un wa la karim" with nominative case (raf'), that is: "he is neither cool nor generous," in the manner of his saying: "So I spend the night, neither troubled (haraj) nor deprived (mahrum)," meaning: I am neither troubled nor deprived.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 56, verse 45:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, they were before that affluent.﴾ This is a causal explanation (ta'lil) for their being afflicted with the punishment mentioned. He took this route in explaining the beginning of the punishment, out of concern to repel the suspicion of injustice in the punishing. Since bestowing reward is something in which there is no suspicion of any deficiency at all, He did not take this approach in it. The affluent (al-mutraf) here, by the indication of the context, is the one who is left to do as he wishes and is not prevented. The meaning is that they were punished because, before the punishment mentioned, they were in the world following the desires of their souls, and there was no restraint from within them to deter them from opposing His commands, mighty and majestic, and committing His prohibitions, glorified is He. Thus it has been said. And it has been said: it is the defiant one (al-'ati), arrogant against accepting the truth and submitting to it. The meaning is that they were punished because they were, in the world, arrogant against accepting what their messengers brought them of faith in Allah, mighty and majestic, and what came from Him, glorified is He. And it has been said: it is the one whom blessing has made affluent, that is, it made him insolent and overbearing. Close to this is what has been said: it is the one given luxury who is immersed in desires. Upon this is the statement of Abu al-Su'ud: that is, they were before what was mentioned of the evil punishment in the world, enjoying blessings of every kind, of foods, drinks, good dwellings and noble residences, immersed in desires; therefore they were punished with their opposites. It has been objected that many of the People of the Left are not affluent in the sense he considered, so how can the punishment of all be explained by that? This objection does not apply to the two statements we previously mentioned, as is not hidden.

Some people explained the affluent by what was mentioned and escaped the objection by saying: explaining the punishment of all by what was mentioned, as a cause, does not require that each of the things mentioned be present in each of the People of the Left; rather, the existence of the group in the group is what is required, and the specification of some with some does not harm this, so consider it. It has also been said: the affluent is the one made to possess luxury (turfa), that is, abundant blessing, and all of them are affluent in relation to the state in which they will be on the Day of Resurrection. This, despite what is in it, does not make the matter of the causal explanation clear.

﴿And they used to persist﴾ — they were obstinate and refused to give it up, and they continued ﴿in the great violation﴾, i.e., the great sin. Some of them interpreted *al-hinth* (violation) as the great sin, not sin in general, and this is supported by the fact that its original meaning is a great injustice, so describing it as "great" is for emphasis in describing its greatness, just as *al-tawd* (a towering mountain), which is itself a great mountain, is described with the same word. What is meant by it, as narrated from Qatada, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd, is polytheism (*shirk*), and this is the apparent meaning.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd recorded from al-Shaʿbi that what is meant is the major sins, and it seems he understood the meaning to be: "and they used to persist in every great violation." In another report from him, it is the *yamin al-ghamus* (the perjurious oath), and its apparent wording is unrestricted. Al-Taj al-Subki said in his *Tabaqat*: "I asked the Shaykh, meaning his father Taqi al-Din, 'What is the great violation?' He said: 'It is swearing an oath to deny the resurrection, which is alluded to by His saying, ﴿And they swore by God their most solemn oaths: God will not raise up one who dies﴾ [An-Nahl: 38].'" This is a good explanation, because although *al-hinth* has been interpreted as sin in general or as great sin, its well-known usage is for failing to fulfil an oath. It has been objected that this is ruled out by the wording.

Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, commentary on surah 56, verses 47–48:

﴿And they used to say, "When we have died and become dust and bones..."﴾ up to the end of the verse. The repetition is necessary (lilluzum al-takrar). It has been answered that the first (statement) describes them as persisting in a false oath, and the second describes them as persisting in denial. The repetition also points to an argument whose invalidity is evident, although there is no objection to repeating what indicates denial. It serves as a preparatory introduction (tawti'ah) and a groundwork (tamhid) for explaining its invalidity.

The meaning of their words "we were dust and bones" is that some of our parts, of flesh, skin and the like, had become dust, and some parts had become decayed bones. Dust is mentioned first because it is further from the life that the matter they are denying, the resurrection, requires.

"Idha" is purely a temporal adverb (mutamahhidah li-l-zharfiyyah). Its governing element is what is indicated by the words of Allah, ﴿Are we indeed to be resurrected?﴾, not "to be resurrected" itself, because there are several things that prevent the element following a word from governing what precedes it, namely "we will be resurrected" (nab'athu). That governing element is the basis of the denial. Restricting it to the stated time does not mean that their denial is limited to it, since they deny being brought back to life after death even if the body is in its (intact) state. Rather, this is to strengthen the denial of resurrection by directing it at a state wholly incompatible with it. This is like an argument made in support of what they claim.

The repetition of the interrogative hamza is to emphasize the rejection (ta'kid al-nakir), and the embellishment of the sentence with "inna" is to emphasize the denial, not to deny the emphasis.

As for His words, glorified is He, ﴿Or our forefathers of old?﴾, it is conjoined (ma'tuf) either to the position (mahall) of "inna" and its subject, or to the concealed pronoun in "mab'uthun". It is permissible because of the separation by the hamza, even though it is a single letter, as al-Zamakhshari said. The governing effect of what precedes this hamza does not harm the word conjoined after it, because it is repeated for emphasis and has been displaced from its place.

The saying of the grammarians, "When a particle is repeated for emphasis, it must be repeated along with what was originally attached to it, or with a pronoun," is not an invariable rule, because of the occurrence of "wa-la li-ma bihim abadan dawa'" and similar examples.

It is also permissible that "aba'una" (our forefathers) is the subject (mubtada'), with its predicate omitted, indicated by what precedes it, meaning "are resurrected" (mab'uthun). The clause would then be a conjunction to the preceding clause. But this is an artificial construction, which is unnecessary given the conjunction mentioned above.

The meaning is: "Will our forefathers also be raised?" The purpose is to add to the sense of improbability. They mean that since they are older, their resurrection is further off and more implausible.

Qalun and Ibn 'Amir read "aw aba'una" with a sukun on the waw. On this reading, it is not conjoined to the pronoun, since there is no separating element.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 56, verses 51–54:**

﴿Then indeed you, O you who go astray, the deniers,﴾ is a coordinate (*ʿaṭf*, grammatical coordination) upon ﴿the first ones﴾ and falls within the scope of speech. "Then" (*thumma*) indicates a temporal or a rank-based sequence. ﴿the deniers﴾ refers to denial of the Resurrection, or to what encompasses it and other things, and it enters the context initially, according to what has been said. The address is to the people of Makkah and their like. ﴿shall surely eat﴾ after the Resurrection, the gathering, and the entry into Hell, ﴿of a tree of zaqqum﴾. The first "min" (*min*, "of") is for the beginning of the limit (*ibtidaʾ al-ghayah*), and the second is for explaining the tree and specifying it, meaning: beginning to eat from a tree that is zaqqum. It is also permitted that the first "min" be partitive (*tabʿid*), and the second "min" remain as it is. It is also permitted that ﴿of zaqqum﴾ be an apposition (*badal*) to His, may He be exalted, words ﴿of a tree﴾, so "min" admits both readings. It has also been said that the first "min" is superfluous (*zaʾidah*). ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) read ﴿min shajarah﴾ (in the singular feminine), and the feminine form is clear in His, may He be exalted, words ﴿and fill your bellies from it﴾, meaning your bellies from the severity of hunger, for it is what compelled them and forced them to eat the like of it, of that which is not eaten.

*[Page 146]*

As for the reading of the majority, its justification is interpretation according to meaning (*al-ḥaml ʿalā al-maʿnā*), because it carries the sense of "a tree" or "trees," if one considers that it applies to the plural. As for the masculine form in this reading, in His, may He be glorified, words ﴿and drink on top of it﴾, meaning immediately after that, without delay, ﴿from boiling water﴾, meaning hot water to the utmost extent, due to the predominance of thirst, it is clear and needs no interpretation. Some have said: the feminine is first in consideration of meaning, and the masculine second in consideration of wording. It was objected to this: that it involves considering the wording after considering the meaning, contrary to what is customary. So if the pronoun mentioned, referring to the tree, were repeated in consideration of its being edible, so that both masculine and feminine would be in consideration of meaning, it would be better. But there is discussion about this. Its justification on the second reading is that the pronoun refers to the zaqqum, or to the tree, in consideration of its being zaqqum, or in consideration of its being edible. It has also been said that it refers absolutely to the eating, and this was criticized as far-fetched, because drinking upon it is not upon its consumption, along with what it involves of dislocating pronouns, and the fact that it is a common and non-misleading metaphor does not remove the far-fetchedness. So reflect.

﴿So you will drink as thirsty camels drink﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah and al-Dahhak said: it is the plural of *ahyam*, which is the camel afflicted with *al-huyam* (هُيام), pronounced with a *damma* on the *ha'*, a disease resembling *istisqa'* (a dropsy-like condition) that afflicts camels so that they keep drinking until they die or fall into severe sickness. It is also said: *ibil hayma'* and *naqa hayma'* (a thirsty camel, female), just as one says *jamal ahyam* (a thirsty male camel). The poet said:

"So I have become like the thirsty (she-camel), for the water does not cool her thirst, and her thirst does not end her suffering."

Some scholars took *al-Hiym* here to be the plural of *al-haya'* (الهَيْماءُ). It was also said that it is the plural of *ha'im* or *ha'ima*, and that the plural of *fa'il* on the pattern *fu'l*, like *bazil* and *buzl*, is irregular (shadhdh). Ibn 'Abbas also said, as did Sufyan, that *al-Hiym* means the sands that do not become saturated with water because of their looseness. Its singular is *hayam*, with a *fatha* on the *ha'* according to the well-known reading, like *sahab* and *suhub*. Then it was lightened, and what happens to the plural of *abyad* was done to it: the *damma* was changed into a *kasra* so that it would be sound with a *ya'*, and the word was lightened, so the *ha'* was given a *kasra* for the sake of the *ya'*. This is a regular analogy in its category. Tha'lab said: it is with a *damma*, like *qurad* and *qird*, then it was lightened and what you have heard was done to it.

As for the conjunction with *fa'* (فَ), it was said that this is because excess comes after the original. It was also said that each of the two conjoined items is more specific than the other: one who drinks boiling water may not have the disease of *al-huyam*, and one who has the disease of *al-huyam* may drink other than boiling water. The kind of drinking that does not bring satisfaction results from drinking boiling water, because it does not quench the thirst. The view preferred by the mufti of the Rumi lands (the Ottoman domains) is that this is like an explanation of what precedes it, meaning: your drinking will not be ordinary drinking, but rather like the drinking of thirsty camels.

*Al-shurb* (الشُّرْبُ) with a *damma* is a verbal noun (masdar), and it was said that it is a noun for what is drunk. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited, as a group of narrators including al-Hakim reported and he authenticated, from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, *shariba* (شَرْبَ) with a *fatha* on the *shin*, which is the verbal noun of *shariba*, the analogical form. With this reading a group of the Seven Readers recited, as did al-A'raj, Ibn al-Musayyab, Shu'ayb, Malik ibn Dinar and Ibn Jurayj. Mujahid and Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi recited with a *kasra* on the *shin* (شِرْبَ), which is a noun meaning what is drunk, not a verbal noun, like *al-tahn* and *al-ra'y*.

This is that which was mentioned of the varieties of punishment, ﴿their nuzul (a welcoming gift or hospitality) on the Day of Religion﴾, that is, the Day of Recompense. If that is their nuzul, which is what is offered to a guest of what is present, then what do you think of what awaits them after the abode has settled for them and the dwelling has become secure for them in the Fire? As for calling it a nuzul, even though a guest is honoured with such things, this contains a mockery (tahakkum) that is not hidden. A parallel to this is his saying:

*And when the tyrant came upon us with his army, we made the spears and the sharp swords his nuzul.*

Ibn Muhaysin, Kharija from Nafi', Nu'aym, Mahbub, Abu Zayd, Harun, Ismah, and Abbas, all of them from Abu 'Amr, read *nuzuluhum* with the letter *zay* pronounced with sukun instead of damma, for lightness, as in the verse of poetry. The sentence is delivered from Him, glorified and exalted be He, by way of a summing-up (fadhlaka), confirming the content of the preceding speech, and it is not included within the scope of "say."

وقَوْلُهُ تَعالى:

﴿Nahnu khalaqnakum falawla tusaddiqun (We created you, so why do you not believe?)﴾ is a shift of address (talwin al-khitab) and a turning of the speech toward the disbelievers by way of rebuke and reproach (al-ilzam wa al-tabkit). The fa' (so) indicates the consequence of the exhortation (al-tahdid) upon what precedes it, meaning: "Why then do you not believe in the creation?" This is indicated by the context of "We created you." Since their belief, which is implied by His words, "And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, 'Allah'" [Luqman: 25; al-Zumar: 38], was not realized, their deeds were treated as nonexistent and as denial, because they were not accompanied by obedience and righteous deeds, but rather by what indicates the opposite, namely polytheism and disobedience. Therefore they were urged to believe in that.

It was also said: the intended meaning is, "Why do you not believe in the resurrection?" because it has been mentioned before, and their denial of it has been mentioned in their saying, "Shall we, when we are bones and dust, indeed be resurrected?" [al-Isra': 49, 98; al-Mu'minun: 82; al-Saffat: 16; al-Waqi'ah: 47]. In that case the speech is a pointer to the inference (al-istidlal) from the initial creation to the return, for whoever is able to originate is necessarily able to bring back. The first view is the more apparent, as will become clear from what follows, God willing.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 56, verse 58:

﴿Have you considered that which you emit?﴾ That is, that which you discharge into the wombs of the drops of semen (nutfah). Ibn ʿAbbas and Abu al-Thimal read «tamnūn» with a fatḥah on the tā', from manā al-nutfata (he emitted the drop), meaning amnāhā, i.e., he expelled it by the propulsion of nature (dafʿ al-ṭabīʿah).

Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, commentary on surah 56, verse 59:

﴿Do you create it?﴾ That is, do you decree it and shape it into a human being, well-formed and complete in its creation? The meaning is then the creation of what comes from it (the semen), on the basis that there is either an elision (*taqdir*) or a metaphor (*tajawwuz*) in the speech. It is also permissible to leave it on its apparent meaning, so that ﴿Do you create it?﴾ means: do you bring into being and originate the very substance of what you emit (*tumnuna*)? ﴿Or are We the Creators?﴾ of it, without anything of yours entering into it. As for *a-ra'aytum* (أرَأيْتُمْ), the discussion of it has already passed more than once. Here it is said that the relative pronoun (*ism al-mawsul*) is its first object, and the interrogative sentence is its second object. The same applies to the similar cases that follow. Where the verb *ra'aytum* means "see" in the sense of sight (*ru'yah basariyyah*), the interrogative sentence after it is an independent resumption (*mustaʼnafah*) with no place in terms of *i'rab* (grammatical case-analysis).

As for *antum* (أنْتُمْ), it is permissible for it to be the subject (*mubtada'*) of a nominal sentence, with the sentence after it as its predicate (*khabar*). It is also permissible for it to be the doer (*fa'il*) of a verb that has been omitted, the original being *a-takhluqunahu* (أتَخْلُقُونَهُ), so that when the verb was dropped the pronoun became detached. Abu Hayyan preferred this view.

As for *am* (أمْ), it has been said to be disjunctive (*munqati'ah*), because what follows it is a full sentence. The meaning would then be "Rather, are We the Creators?", with the interrogative used for affirmation (*taqrir*). Some grammarians said it is conjunctive (*muttasilah*) and equivalent to the *hamzah* (أ) (*mu'adilah lil-hamzah*), as if it were said: ﴿Do you create it, or are We?﴾ Then *al-Khaliqun* (الخالِقُونَ) was brought after it as an emphatic repetition (*ta'kid*), not as a predicate in its own right.

﴿We have decreed death among you﴾: We divided it among you and fixed the death of each person at a specific time, as Our will requires, a will founded on far-reaching wisdom. Ibn Kathir read "qadarna" with a light pronunciation (takhfif). ﴿And We are not to be outdone﴾: that is, no one can overpower Us. ﴿In replacing your likenesses﴾: that is, in destroying you and bringing in others like you from creation in your place. Thus "sabq" (outdoing) is a metaphor for "ghalaba" (overpowering), either as an explicit metaphor (isti'ara tasrihiyya) or as a metonymic metaphor (majaz mursal) for its consequence. The apparent sense of the words of some eminent scholars is that it is literal when it takes "ʿalā" (on/over). The clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relative to the pronoun in "qadarna." It seems the meaning is: We decreed this while We are able to cause you to die all at once and to create others like you.

﴿And We will bring you into being in what you do not know﴾: of creation and of states (atwar) that you are not accustomed to. Al-Hasan said: from your being monkeys and swine. Perhaps this interpretation was chosen because the verse tends toward a warning. The meaning is: and We are able to do this as well. It is also permissible that "amthalukum" is the plural of "mathal" (with two fathas), meaning "attribute" (sifa), not the plural of "mithl" (with sukun), meaning "likeness" (shabah), as in the first interpretation. That is: We are able to change the attributes you have, both in form and in character, and bring you into being in attributes you do not know. It has also been said: the meaning is that We will bring you into being at the Resurrection in forms other than your forms in this world. It has been said: the meaning is that no one outruns Us so as to flee from death or to alter the time We have appointed for it. Here the intent is to liken the state of one who is spared from death or whose term is delayed beyond its appointed time to the state of one who is pursued by a pursuer but is not caught and outstrips him. The words of Allah, Exalted is He, ﴿in replacing﴾ and so on, are in the position of a circumstantial clause relative to the hidden pronoun in "masbuqin," meaning: while We are capable of, or resolved upon, replacing your likenesses. The preceding clause remains as it is.

Al-Tabari said: "in replacing" is connected to "qadarna" and is its cause (ʿilla), and the clause "and We are not to be outdone" is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ). The meaning is: We decreed death among you in order that We might replace your likenesses, that is, We cause a group to die and replace it with another group, generation after generation in this manner.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 56, verse 65:

﴿Had We willed, We could have made it ujaj (أُجاجًا)﴾: salty, brackish, undrinkable. It derives from al-ajij (الأجيج), the blazing of fire. It is said that al-ujaj is anything that stings the mouth and cannot be drunk, so it includes salt, bitterness, and heat. Either this is what is meant, or salt is meant by context. The lam (the emphatic lam, اللام) is omitted from the answer of "law" (لو) here because of the verbal and situational indicators. Whenever omission is permitted, as in the verse of Aws:

*Until, when the dogs said to her, "Like today, one pursued and no pursuer,"*

I have not seen (this objection raised)... The indicator here is situational, so it is more fitting that omitting it alone be permitted, as al-Zamakhshari established. He also established another view, whose upshot is that the lam is merely for emphasis, and so it suits the context of emphasis. It was therefore inserted in the verse about food and not drink, to indicate that the matter of food takes precedence over the matter of drink, and that the threat of losing it is more severe and grave, since drink follows it. Do you not see that a guest is given drink after being fed? The physicians have mentioned that water is digestive. This is supported by placing food before drink in the sublime arrangement. The Imam has a lengthy discussion on this point, in which he objected to al-Zamakhshari and explained the reason for mentioning the lam in one case and omitting it in the other. I have not found that it provides satisfactory clarity. Better in my view is the statement of Ibn al-Athir in *al-Mathal al-Sa'ir*: the lam was inserted in the food and not the drink because turning sweet water into salt is easier to achieve in custom and habit, and salty water is found more commonly than sweet water. Often, when sweet waters flow over lands of salty soil, they turn it into brackishness. So turning sweet water into salt does not require added emphasis, and therefore the lam of emphasis, which adds confirmation, is not inserted. As for food, turning it into crumbs is among the things outside the usual, and when it happens it comes from intense wrath. Therefore it is joined with the lam to establish its occurrence and affirm its matter. End of quotation.

﴿Then will you not give thanks?﴾ This is an exhortation to give thanks for all of it, because that is more beneficial than thanks for the sweetness of water alone, as some have held.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 56, verse 73:

﴿We have made it a reminder﴾. This is a specific resumption (isti'naf) concerning its benefits. That is, We made it a reminder of the Fire of Hell, since We attached to it the means of livelihood so that they would look at it and be reminded by it of what they were promised. Or it means: We made it a reminder and a model (unmudhaj) of Hell, because of what is in the two Sahihs and others from Abu Hurayrah, who said that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "This fire of yours that you kindle is one part of seventy parts of the fire of Hell." On both interpretations, "tadhkirah" derives from dhikr, the opposite of forgetfulness. In the first interpretation, the fire is not considered to be of the same kind as the fire of Hell at first, whereas in the second it is considered so. It has also been said: it is a insight (tabsirah) regarding the matter of Resurrection, because whoever brings out fire from the green tree, which is its opposite, is capable of restoring what its components have scattered. It has also been said: it is an insight in darkness, by whose light one sees. But in this there is the objection that tadhkirah does not mean tabsirah, which is derived from basar (sight). That the intended meaning is "a reminder of the Fire of Hell" is what is transmitted from many, among them Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah.

﴿and a provision﴾, that is, a benefit, ﴿for those who travel﴾. Those who travel are the ones who go down into the qiwa, which is the desert. One says: "aqwa al-rajul" (he entered the qiwa), as "asḥara" means he entered the ṣaḥrā' (open desert). The specification of "al-muqwin" for this is because they are in greatest need of it, for those who are settled or who stay nearby are not compelled to strike flint.

It has also been said: ﴿al-muqwin﴾ means the travellers. This was narrated by a group from Ibn Abbas, and by Abd ibn Humayd from al-Hasan. It was also narrated by Ibn Jarir and Abd al-Razzaq from Qatadah, with the addition: "How many a people have travelled and then run out of provisions, so they kindled a fire, warmed themselves by it and benefited from it." The application of "al-muqwin" to travellers is because they often traverse the desolate lands and the deserts. It has also been said: ﴿al-muqwin﴾ means the poor, who light themselves with it in darkness and warm themselves against the cold, as if the state of one who is in the desert was imagined as poverty, so it is said: "aqwa fulan," meaning he became poor, like their saying "atraba" and "armala." Ibn Zayd said: it means the hungry, because their bellies and their provision-bags have been emptied of food, so they need it to cook what they eat. They were specified, as it is said, because others enjoy it without making it a provision. This has been criticised as being far-fetched, since what concerns them and fills their need is not restricted to what is eaten only after cooking.

Ikrimah and Mujahid said: ﴿al-muqwin﴾ means those who benefit from it among all people, the travellers and the residents, who light themselves by it, warm themselves against the cold, and benefit from it in cooking and baking. Al-Allamah al-Tibi and al-Tabarsi said: according to this view, "al-muqwi" is one of the words with two opposite meanings. It is said of the poor man "muqwin," because he is empty of wealth, and of the rich man "muqwin," because of his strength to do what he wants. One says: "aqwa al-rajul" when he came to a state of strength. The meaning is a provision for both the rich and the poor, because none of them can do without it. End of quotation.

In this there is a point that is not hidden, and perhaps the closer meaning according to it is that "al-iqwa" was intended as need, and the one who benefits from it is in need of it, so reflect on this. The postponement of this benefit is to draw attention to the fact that the more important is the otherworldly benefit. The mention of water before fire is because the need for it is more intense and greater, and benefiting from it is more general and abundant.

Some have said: the matter of the creation of man from a drop (nutfah) is mentioned first, because the blessing in that is prior to the blessing in the three that follow. Then after it is mentioned what sustains man, namely the benefit of tillage, which is food, without which a living body cannot do without. That is the grain that is baked, and after its acquisition it needs water to knead it, so water is mentioned after it. Then fire is mentioned to turn it into bread, so fire is mentioned after water. This is, as you see, far-fetched.

Some have found it good for the reciter to say, after each interrogative sentence among the preceding sentences: "Rather, You, O Lord." Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Hajar al-Marwi:

He said: I spent the night with Ali, may God honour his face. I heard him praying at night, reciting. He came to this verse: ﴿Have you considered the semen you emit?﴾ ﴿Is it you who create it, or are We the Creator?﴾ and he said: "Rather, You, O Lord," three times. Then he recited ﴿Is it you who send it down from the rain-cloud, or are We the senders-down?﴾ and he said: "Rather, You, O Lord," three times. Then he recited ﴿Is it you who produce its tree, or are We the producers?﴾ and he said: "Rather, You, O Lord," three times.

And you know that there is a difference among the scholars regarding the approval of saying the like of that in prayer.

﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾ is ordered upon what has been enumerated of the wonders of His creation, Mighty and Majestic, and the deposits of His blessings, Glorified and Exalted. It is said that the meaning is as follows: the glorification (*tasbih*, the declaration of God's transcendence above all imperfection) was renewed, with the transitive verb being placed in the position of the intransitive, and what is meant by its renewal is its continuation, not its bringing into being, because the blessed Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, was never turning away from it. Al-Tibi (*al-Tibi*) criticized this, saying that it is the opposite of what the word "renewal" requires, so what is meant is the renewal of the glorification. In the speech there is an ellipsis, i.e. "glorify by mentioning the name of your Lord," or the "name" is a metaphor for the mention (*dhikr*), since applying the name to a thing is mentioning it. The *ba'* (in *bi-smi*) is for seeking help or for association, and that it is for transitivity, as the apparent sense of Abu Hayyan's speech implies, is not correct. *Al-'Azim* (the Mighty) is an attribute of the name, or of the Lord.

The placing of the command to glorify after what has been enumerated is either to declare Him far exalted above what those who deny His oneness say, those who disbelieve in His blessings despite their greatness and abundance, or as thanks for those previous blessings, since declaring Him transcendent and magnifying Him, Majestic and Exalted, after mentioning His blessings, Glorified and Exalted, is praise for them, and so it is in reality thanks to the Bestower. Or it is for expressing amazement at the matter of the disbelievers in disregarding those dazzling blessings, despite their lofty rank and the clarity of their matter. *Subhan* is used to express amazement as a well-known figurative usage, so *sabbaha* means "he marvelled," and its origin is "say *subhan Allah* in amazement." But this is far-fetched, and what came before is more apparent.

That said, it is also permitted that there is no ellipsis in "*bi-smi rabbika*" and no metaphor, but that it remains on its apparent meaning. They have said regarding His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ (87:1): just as the essence of God, Exalted is He, and His attributes, Glorified is He, must be declared free of deficiencies, the words coined for them must also be declared free of bad manners, and this is more eloquent, because it necessarily entails the sanctification of His essence, Mighty and Majestic, by way of priority, through the symbolic allusion (*kinaya ramziyya*). In this there is the point that this is only attainable if the *ba'* is not mentioned, and making it superfluous is contrary to the apparent sense, and its being for transitivity you have already heard. Some of them, on this view, made the address non-specific, saying: when He, Exalted is He, mentioned what He mentioned of the matters, and all of them acknowledged that they are from God, Exalted is He, and when the disbelievers were asked to affirm oneness, they would say: "We do not associate in meaning, rather we take idols as gods," and that is association in the name, and "the One who created us and created the heavens and the earth is God, Exalted is He, so we declare Him transcendent in reality," He, Glorified is He, said: ﴿So glorify by the name of your Lord﴾, in the sense of: just as you, O heedless one, have acknowledged that they do not share in reality, acknowledge that they do not share in the name, and do not call anything other than Him, Exalted is He, a god, for the name follows the meaning and the reality. So the address is like the address in the words of the preacher: "O wretched one, you have spent your life and did not set right your affair," where he does not mean any specific person, but means "O wretched listener." And this, as you see, is far-fetched. Yes, the possibility that the address is general is not to be denied, but this explanation is not binding on it.

Then, the apparent meaning of mentioning the Lord, or mentioning His name, Glorified is He, as established previously, is what is most immediately understood and well known.

In *al-Kashf*, it is said that what is meant by this is the recitation of the Qur'an by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or of this noble surah, which includes proof of the Resurrection, of recompense, and of the degrees of its people, so that His words after it may apply to it: ﴿So I swear﴾. According to the first view, there must be an ellipsis, i.e. "so glorify by the name of your Lord and comply with what you were commanded," then "I swear that it is indeed a Qur'an." The purpose is to emphasize the command to glorify. I say: the application to the apparent meaning is also attainable, except that an ellipsis is required in the speech. There is no harm in saying that when He, Exalted is He, mentioned what He mentioned of the great blessings that call to His oneness, Glorified is He, and to describing Him with what befits Him, Mighty and Majestic, He said, Glorified is He: ﴿So glorify by the name of your Lord﴾, meaning: declare Him, Exalted is He, free of what they say in describing Him, Glorified is He, and turn to warning them with the Qur'an and arguing against them with it, after arguing with what we have mentioned: ﴿So I swear that it is indeed a Qur'an﴾, such and such.

As for *fa-*, in His words, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿fa-lā uqsimu﴾ ("So I do not swear"), the *lā* is extra, for emphasis, like the one in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿li-allā ya'lama ahl al-kitāb﴾ ("so that the People of the Book may know," al-Hadid: 29). To this is the poet's line:

*liyaʿlam rabbī anna baytiya wāsiʿ*
("So that my Lord may know that my house is spacious.")

In that case it is not correct for the verb to be joined with the emphatic *nūn* (*al-nūn al-muʾakkada*), because it would make it specific to the future, which is contrary to the intended meaning. What Ibn ʿUsfur and the Basrans preferred is that a present-tense verb, as here, may not be sworn upon. Whenever the future is intended from the verb, the emphatic *nūn* must be attached to it, so it is said: *la-uqsimanna* ("I will surely swear"), and its omission is very weak. From this, they took the reading of al-Hasan and ʿIsa to be that the *lam* is the *lam* of inception (*lam al-ibtidāʾ*), and the subject (*mubtadaʾ*) is omitted, because it does not enter upon the verb. The estimated reading is *fa-la-anā uqsimu* ("So indeed I swear"). It was also said that the reading of the majority is similar to this, on the basis that the *alif* was produced from the prolongation of the vowel. This was objected to on the grounds that when the subject enters upon it the *lam* of inception, its omission is either impossible or ugly, because its entry is for emphasis of it, and that calls for giving it attention, while its omission indicates the opposite.

Saʿid ibn Jubayr and some grammarians said: *lā* is a negation and a rejection of what the disbelievers say about the Qur'an, that it is sorcery, poetry, and soothsaying. It is as if it was said: "There is no validity to what they say about it." Then it was resumed, and it was said: ﴿uqsimu﴾ ("I swear"), etc. Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that it is not permissible, because it involves omitting the subject and predicate of *lā* outside the context of an answer to a question, like *lā* in answer to "Is there anyone in the house?"

It was also said: the better view, when *lā* is intended as a negation for something omitted, and what follows it is a fresh statement, is to bring the *wāw* in speech, as in *lā*, *wa-aṭāla Allāhu baqāʾaka* ("No, and may God prolong your life"). Some have said that *lā* is often placed before an oath as an opening, as in the line:

*lā wa-abīki ibnata al-ʿāmirī* ∗∗∗ *lā yadda'ī al-qawmu annī afirru*
("No, by your father, daughter of al-ʿAmiri! The people do not claim that I flee.")

Abu Muslim and a group said: the statement is upon its apparent, obvious meaning, and the sense is: "I do not swear," because the matter is clearer than needing an oath, that is, it does not need any oath at all, let alone this great oath. Therefore, the claim of the Mufti of the Ottoman lands, that the choice of the sworn-by thing and its exaltation is inconsistent with this, arises from heedlessness, as is not hidden from a discerning person.

﴿bi-mawāqiʿ al-nujūm﴾ ("by the setting-places of the stars"), that is, by the falling places of the stars of the sky and their sunsets, as came in a report from Qatadah and al-Hasan, on the basis that *al-wuqūʿ* means falling and setting. Its being specified for the oath is because in their setting there is the disappearance of their trace, and an indication of the existence of a constant influence that does not change. For this reason, Khalil, peace be upon him, reasoned from the setting to the existence of the Maker, Majestic and Exalted is He. Or it is because that is the time for those who pray at night and those who supplicate to Him, Exalted is He, and the time of the descent of mercy and pleasure upon them.

Al-Bukhari and Muslim have reported from Abu Hurayrah, as a marfuʿ report (traced to the Prophet, ﷺ): "Our Lord descends every night to the lowest heaven when the last third of the night remains. He says: 'Who calls upon Me, so that I may answer him? Who asks of Me, so that I may give him? Who seeks My forgiveness, so that I may forgive him?'"

And from al-Hasan also: the meaning is their setting-places at the time of their dispersal on the Day of Resurrection. It was said: *mawqiʿ* in it is a noun of place (*maṣdar mīmī*) or a noun of time. Perhaps their falling on that day is not all at once. The specification is because in that there is the manifestation of His great majesty, Mighty and Majestic is He, and the realization of what the disbelievers deny about the Resurrection.

From Abu Jaʿfar and Abu ʿAbd Allah, peace be upon their forefathers and upon them both, the meaning is their setting-places at the time of the swooping down upon those who steal hearing from the devils. The reality of this swooping has already been explained to you, so do not be heedless. It was also said: the setting-places of the stars are the *anwāʾ* (weather-stars), which the Jahiliyyah claimed they were given rain by. Perhaps this is taken from some of the reports concerning the occasion of revelation, which we will mention, God willing. It is not explicit in the intended meaning of the *anwāʾ*, but it is permissible that the setting-places in general be intended.

[Page 153]

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir reported from Qatadah that they are its stations and its courses, on the basis that *al-wuqūʿ* means descent, as is said: "You fell upon the one who knows" (*ʿalā al-khabīr saqaṭta*), and this is common. The specification is because He, Exalted is He, has in that evidence of His great power and perfect wisdom that the scope of expression cannot encompass.

A group, including Ibn ʿAbbas, said: the stars are the stars of the Qur'an, and their setting-places are the times of their descent.

Al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shuʿab* reported from him that he said: "The Qur'an was sent down on the Night of Power (*Laylat al-Qadr*) from the highest heaven to the lowest heaven all at once, then it was revealed in parts over the years." In another wording: "Then it descended from the lowest heaven to the earth in stars (*nujūman*), then he recited: ﴿fa-lā uqsimu bi-mawāqiʿ al-nujūm﴾."

This view is supported by the fact that the pronoun in His words after this, ﴿innahu la-qurʾān﴾ ("indeed it is a Qur'an"), then refers to what is understood from the setting-places of the stars, so much so that it is almost counted as explicitly mentioned, and there is no need to say that the context explains it, as in the other views. The aspect of specification is clearer than to be hidden. Perhaps the speech about it is of the type of "Your front teeth, indeed they are like unripe colocynth" (*wa-thanāyāka innahā ighrīḍ*).

Ibn ʿAbbas and the people of Madinah, Hamzah, and al-Kisaʾi read *bi-mawqiʿ* in the singular, with the plural intended.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 56, verse 76–77:

﴿And indeed, it is an oath, if you knew, great﴾ includes an interjection (i'tiraadh, parenthetical insertion) within another. So His saying, exalted is He, "Indeed, it is an oath, great" (innahu la-qasamun 'azim), is a parenthetical interjection between the oath and that which is sworn to, which is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an﴾. It is an exaltation of the oath, confirming and emphasizing it. And His saying, mighty and majestic is He, ﴿if you knew﴾, is a parenthetical interjection between the attribute and the thing described, and it is an emphasis upon that exaltation. The answer to (law, "if") is either omitted, intended to negate their knowledge, or elided, relying on its being evident, meaning: "you would have glorified it" or "you would have acted in accordance with its requirement."

As for the aspect of that oath being great, it has been indicated earlier, or it is evident on the basis that what is meant by ﴿the places of the stars﴾ is what has been related from Ibn 'Abbas and the group. The meaning of the Qur'an being noble (karim) is that it is good and approved in its genre among books, or that it is beneficial, abundant in benefits. And how could it not be, when it includes the fundamental sciences important for the reform of livelihood and the hereafter? The nobility (karam) in this sense is figurative, as al-Tibi said, derived from the well-known nobility (karam).

It has been said: karam is more general than abundance of giving and benevolence, and than being characterized by praiseworthy qualities, such as abundance of benefit, for that is a praiseworthy attribute, so its being karam is literal. It is also permissible that what is meant is "noble with Allah, exalted is He." It has been said: this returns to what preceded, and it contains an unnecessary estimation. In any case, the focus of the benefit is the mentioned attribute. It has been said: the referent of the pronoun is the Qur'an, not insofar as it bears the title of being a Qur'an; so by merely informing about it that it is a Qur'an the benefit is achieved, meaning: indeed, it is what is recited upon the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, not that he composed it, as the disbelievers claimed.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 56, verse 78:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿In a Book well-guarded﴾ is another description of the Qur'an, meaning: it exists in a Book protected from anyone other than the angels brought near (may peace be upon them), so that none besides them can gain access to it. Thus what is intended is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), as related from al-Rabi' ibn Anas and others. It has also been said: meaning, in a Book protected from alteration and change, namely the codex (mushaf) that is in the hands of the Muslims. This includes the report of the unseen, since at that time there were no mushafs. Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Ikrimah that he said: "In a Book" means the Torah and the Gospel. This was transmitted in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit), and then he said: "It is as if it was said: it is mentioned in a Book well-guarded, its nobility and honour." So the meaning according to this is citing the revealed Books. End of quote.

It is apparent that on this view the word "Book" is intended as a genus, so that the intention of the Torah and the Gospel is valid. Describing it as "well-guarded" carries some obscurity; perhaps what is intended is its lofty status and great worth, since concealment is almost a necessary attribute of a noble thing. It is also permissible to intend this figurative meaning on views other than this one.
Page 154
It has been said: the "well-guarded Book" is the heart of the believer. But this is, as you see, far-fetched.

It has also been said: what is meant by its being "in a well-guarded Book" is only that it is protected from change and alteration, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed, We are its guardians﴾ [Yusuf: 63]. But what is relied upon is what has preceded. It is also permitted for the prepositional phrase to be connected to "noble" (karim), as one says "Zayd is noble in himself." The meaning would then be that it is noble in the Preserved Tablet, even if it is not noble in the eyes of the disbelievers. The descriptive form is more eloquent, as is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 56, verse 79:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿None touch it except the purified﴾ may be a second attribute (ṣifah) after another attribute of a Book (kitāb), by which is meant the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh). Thus "the purified" (al-muṭahharūn) refers to the angels, peace be upon them, meaning those purified and exalted above the turbidity of nature (kadar al-ṭabī'ah) and the defilement of carnal desires (dans al-ḥuẓūẓ al-nafsiyyah). It has also been said: above the turbidity of bodies and the defilement of matter (hayūlā). The purification in both cases is a spiritual purification, and the negation of its touching is a metonymy (kināyah) for its necessary consequence, which is the negation of access to it and to what is in it.

Or it may be another attribute of the Qur'an. In that case "the purified" means those purified from the minor ritual impurity (ḥadath aṣghar) and the major ritual impurity (ḥadath akbar), taking purity in its legal (shar'iyyah) sense. The meaning is: none should touch the Qur'an except one who is in a state of purity from people. The negation here is similar to what is in the saying of Exalted God: ﴿The adulterer marries none but an adulteress﴾ [al-Nur: 3], and the saying of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace: "A Muslim is the brother of a Muslim; he does not wrong him," etc. It has the sense of a prohibition (nahy), indeed more emphatic than an explicit prohibition. This is one of the reasons they gave for deviating from making "lā" prohibitive. The second reason is that the apparent reading is that the sentence is an attribute, and the basic form of an attribute is that it be a declarative sentence (khabariyyah); there is no need to consider it an imperative (inshā'iyyah) and resort to interpretation. The third is that what is apparent from the ḍammah is that it is an inflection (i'rāb), so reading it otherwise causes confusion. The fourth is that 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) read "mā yamassuhu," and this supports that "lā" is negating. That the meaning of "the purified" is the angels, peace be upon them, is related through several chains from Ibn 'Abbas, and likewise a group transmitted it from Anas, Qatadah, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Abu al-'Aliyah and others. However, some reports from some of these contain what clearly indicates that the pronoun in "yamassuhu," while "the purified" means the angels, peace be upon them, refers to the Qur'an.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Qatadah that he said: "In the verse, that is with the Lord of the worlds: none touch it except the purified among the angels. But as for with you, it is touched by the polytheist and the impure, and the hypocrite, the foul." Al-Bukhari and Muslim reported it, as did Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ma'rifah, from al-Habr, who said: "In the verse, the Book sent down in heaven: none touch it except the angels." What points to this is what Ibn al-Mundhir reported from al-Nu'aymi, who said: Malik said: "The best I have heard concerning this verse, ﴿None touch it except the purified﴾, is that it is in the same position as the verse in 'Abasa: ﴿Nay, indeed it is a reminder. So whoever wills may remember it. In honoured scrolls, exalted, purified, by the hands of scribes, noble and dutiful﴾ ['Abasa: 11–16]." That the intended meaning is those purified from ritual impurities is related from Muhammad al-Baqir, upon his fathers and upon him be peace, and from 'Ata', Tawus and Salim.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, reported from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd who said: "We were with Salman (meaning al-Farisi), may God be pleased with him, when he set off on a need and went out of our sight. Then he came out to us, and we said: 'If you performed ablution, we would ask you about some matters of the Qur'an.' He said: 'Ask me, for I do not touch it; only the purified touch it,' then he recited: ﴿None touch it except the purified﴾."

It has also been said: the sentence is an attribute of the Qur'an, and by "the purified" is meant those purified from disbelief (kufr), and "touch" (massa) is a metaphor for seeking (talab), like "touch" in the saying of Exalted God: ﴿And we sought (lamasna) the heaven﴾ [al-Jinn: 8], meaning none seeks it except the ones purified from disbelief. I have not seen this related from any of the early scholars (salaf), and the negation upon it remains on its apparent sense. A group preferred making the sentence a description of the Qur'an, because the discourse is directed at its sanctity and glorification, not at the status of the hidden Book, though glorifying it entails glorifying that. Al-Imam (al-Razi) declared making it a description of the Book sound, but there is room for debate. On the view that it describes the Qur'an, those who went this way chose to interpret "the purified" as those purified from both major and minor impurity.

In al-Ahkam by al-Jalal al-Suyuti: al-Shafi'i used the verse as evidence for prohibiting one in a state of impurity (muhdith) from touching the mushaf, and this is apparent in preferring that view, though the possibility remains that the sentence describes the Hidden Book or the Qur'an. Most scholars, on the view that "the purified" means the honoured angels, peace be upon them, as you have heard from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah, turned away from using the verse for this ruling and instead used reports as evidence. Imam Malik, 'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Dawud and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr from his father who said: "In the letter of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, to 'Amr ibn Hazm: 'Do not touch the Qur'an except in a state of purity.'"

al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both, who said: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: 'None touches the Qur'an except one who is pure,'" and other reports to that effect. Some said: the prohibition of touching the Qur'an by one not pure may be derived from the verse on the other two possibilities too, because it expresses the magnification of the Qur'an's status and its nobility, and touching without purity impairs its glorification, so the verse rejects it. But this is as you see. Al-Imam extended the discussion at this point at length, the weakness of which is not hidden from one who consults it. Yes, there is no doubt that the verse indicates the great status of the Qur'an, and this entails care for its status. That care is not confined to prohibiting one who is not pure from touching it, but takes many forms, such as increasing its recitation, performing ablution for it, and that a person should not recite while his mouth is ritually unclean, which is disliked (makruh).

It has been said that this is prohibited (ḥarām), like touching it with a defiled hand; and that recitation should take place in a clean place, with the reciter facing the qiblah, humble, with calm and dignity, lowering his head; using the miswak before recitation; proper articulation (tartil); reflection (tadabbur); weeping or feigning weeping; beautifying the voice in recitation; not making it a means of livelihood; and taking care not to forget any verse one has been given of it. Abu Dawud and others reported: "The sins of my community were displayed before me, and I saw no sin greater than a surah of the Qur'an or a verse that a man was given and then forgot." And that one should not have intercourse in its presence, and if one wishes to have intercourse, one should conceal it; that one should not place other heavenly books or other books above it; and that one should not turn its pages with a finger upon which there is saliva that comes off it, for it has been said that one who does this is to be considered a disbeliever, along with other matters mentioned in their proper places. There is disagreement over whether the reciter must be free of ritual impurities. On the authority of Ibn 'Abbas in one report, it is permissible for one in janabah to recite the Qur'an, and this is also related from Imam Abu Hanifah. From Ibn 'Umar: "It is more beloved to me that none recite except one who is pure." It seems they regarded it like other invocations, and the distinction is as clear as the sun.

'Isa read "al-muṭhharūn" as a passive participle with the hamzah of "aṭhara" (causative), lightened; it is related from Nafi' and Abu 'Amr. Salman al-Farisi, may God be pleased with him, read "al-muṭahhirūn," with the ṭā' lightened and the hā' doubled and vowelled with kasrah, as an active participle from "ṭahhara," meaning (the purifiers) themselves, or others by seeking forgiveness for them and inspiring them. Also from him: "al-muṭṭahhirūn," with both doubled, its original form being "al-mutaṭahhirūn," the tā' being assimilated into the ṭā' after being converted into it. It is related from al-Hasan and 'Abd Allah ibn 'Awn, and it has been read "al-mutaṭahhirūn" in the original form.

﴿A revelation from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ This is another attribute of the Qur'an, meaning that it is "revealed" (munazzal). Alternatively, it is a description using the verbal noun (masdar, the noun of action) *tanzil*, because it is revealed in installments (nujum) from among the other books of God, Exalted is He, so it is, in itself, a *tanzil* (revelation). For this reason it is treated like some of its names, so one says: "It came in the *Tanzil* such-and-such," and "the *Tanzil* said such-and-such."

It is also permitted that it be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "it is a *tanzil*," by way of *isti'naf* (resumption, beginning a new sentence). It was also read as *تَنْزِيلًا* in the accusative, meaning *نُزِّلَ تَنْزِيلًا* ("it was sent down as a revelation").

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 56, verse 81:

﴿Is it this discourse﴾ meaning: Do you turn away from this discourse, ﴿this discourse﴾ whose sublime attributes are mentioned, which necessitate its exaltation, reverence, and belief in what it contains and what it guides to, namely the Noble Qur'an, ﴿that you are disparaging?﴾ — i.e., treating it lightly, like one who is "yadhin" (softens, makes soft) in a matter, meaning he makes its side pliant and does not stand firm in it, out of contempt for it. The root of idhan ( idhān, "to be lax, to soften"), as it has been said, is making a hide or the like "madhhun" (oiled, greased) with some oil. Since that makes something soft and pliant in a tangible way, the term is used to denote moral softness; either it is a metaphor for absolute softness, or it is borrowed for it. For this reason, conciliatory dealing (mudarah) is called mudahanah (flattery, accommodation), and this is a well-known metaphor, and because of its fame it became a customary literal meaning. For this reason it is also used here metaphorically for negligence, because the one who is negligent about a matter

does not stand firm in it. And from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Zajjaj: ﴿mudhinun﴾ means "deniers" (mukadhdhibun), and interpreting it thus is because denial is among the branches of negligence.

And from Mujahid: i.e., hypocrites in their affirmation of it, saying to the believers, "We believe in it," and when you are alone with your fellows, you say, "Indeed we are with you." The address then is to the hypocrites, but what we have presented earlier is more preferable, and according to it the address is to the disbelievers, as the context requires.

It is also permitted that by this discourse is meant what they spoke of earlier, in His saying, glorified is He: "And they used to say, 'When we die and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected? And our forefathers of old?'" (al-Waqi'ah: 47–48). So the speech returns to that after refuting it, as if it were said: Is it this discourse you speak of in denying resurrection, that you are disparaging — that is, you know its opposite and say it out of flattery, or are you resolved upon it and determined to persist in it? Its remoteness is not hidden, and it contradicts the occasion of revelation, which you will know shortly, God willing, Exalted is He.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 56, verse 82:**

﴿And you make your provision﴾ (your thanks) ﴿that you deny﴾, meaning: you say, "We were given rain by such-and-such a mansion (nawʾ) of the moon and such-and-such a star." Imam Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sound (hasan), al-Diya in al-Mukhtara, and a group of others related this from ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, from the Prophet (ﷺ). Either this is an indication from him (ﷺ) that the sentence contains an implied genitive (mudaf muqaddar), meaning "the thanks for your provision," or it is an indication that "provision" is used metaphorically for its necessary consequence, which is thanks. Al-Haytham ibn ʿAdi related that among the dialect of Azd Shanuʾa is the phrase "ruziqa fulan fulanan," meaning "he thanked him." It is reported from al-Kirmani that in his commentary on al-Bukhari he mentioned that "provision" (rizq) is among the names of thanks, but he considered this unlikely. Perhaps this is what al-Haytham related. In al-Bahr and elsewhere it is mentioned that ʿAli and Ibn ʿAbbas read "your thanks" (shukrakum) instead of "your provision" (rizqakum). Some commentators of al-Bukhari took this as an explanation (tafsir) rather than as a recitation variant, but this is contrary to the apparent meaning. Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Sulami who said: "ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, recited al-Waqiʿa at the dawn prayer and said: ﴿And you make your thanks﴾ ﴿that you deny﴾. When he finished he said: 'I know that someone will say, why did he recite it this way? I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recite it thus. They used to say, when they were given rain, "We were given rain by such-and-such a mansion," so Allah revealed: ﴿And you make your thanks that when you are given rain you deny﴾.'"

The meaning of making their thanks into denial is that denial is placed in the position of thanks, as if they had fixed it for themselves in that way. It is thus of the type of "their greeting among them is a painful blow," and from it is the saying of the rajaz poet:

"The thanks of the people at the time of favours was the cauterising of sound [limbs] and the gouging of eyes."

Most of the reports indicate that the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿And you make﴾ etc., were revealed concerning those who say "We were given rain by such-and-such a mansion," without reference to what precedes it.

Muslim, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "The people were given rain in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Some of the people have become thankful and some have become disbelievers.' They said: 'This is mercy that Allah has placed.' Some of them said: 'Such-and-such a mansion has spoken truly.' So this verse was revealed: ﴿So I swear by the places of the stars﴾ [al-Waqiʿa 75], up to ﴿And you make your provision that you deny﴾."

Ibn ʿAsakir in his history related something similar from ʿA'isha, may Allah be pleased with her. This occurred, as Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu ʿUrwa, may Allah be pleased with him, during the expedition of Tabuk: "They halted at al-Hijr, and the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded them not to carry any of its water. Then they set off and halted at another place, with no water with them. They complained of this to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he stood up and prayed two rak'as, then supplicated, and they were given rain and watered. A man from the Ansar, who was accused of hypocrisy, said: 'We were only given rain by such-and-such a mansion,' and so what was revealed was revealed." Perhaps a group of disbelievers also said something similar, indeed they continued to say it. The reports agree that the verse concerns those who attribute rain to the mansions. Indeed Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "The exegetes (mufassirun) unanimously agreed that it is a rebuke to those people." The apparent opposition of thanks to disbelief in the preceding hadith suggests that the intended disbelief is ingratitude for a blessing when it is attributed to other than its Creator, may His majesty be exalted. It has indeed been authentically reported alongside faith. al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and others related from Zayd ibn Khalid al-Juhani who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led us in the dawn prayer at al-Hudaybiya, after a rain that had fallen during the night. When he finished he turned to us and said: 'Do you know what your Lord said this night?' They said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'He said: I have not bestowed upon My servants any blessing except that a group of them become disbelievers in it. As for the one who believes in Me and praises Me for My watering, he is the one who believes in Me and disbelieves in the stars. As for the one who says, "We were given rain by such-and-such a mansion," he is the one who believes in the star and disbelieves in Me.'"

According to the view that the verse was revealed concerning those who say that, the verse clearly shows the disbelief that stands opposite to faith. They were saying it out of a belief that the stars are effective in truth, creating the rain, and this is undoubtedly disbelief. This is unlike saying it while believing that it is from the bounty of Allah, the Exalted. The nawʾ (mansion of the moon, the rising or setting of a star marking a time) is only a timing and a sign of rain, and so it is not disbelief. It is said that calling it disbelief is because it leads to disbelief if one believes that it is truly effective.

Furthermore, it has been said: the meaning of the verse, ﴿And you make your thanks﴾ for the blessing of the Qur'an, ﴿that you deny﴾ it. This is indicated by what Qatada related from al-Hasan: "How evil is what these people took for themselves! They were given from the Book of Allah the Exalted only denial."

In al-Irshad it is said that this is more suitable to the context and sequence of the noble composition. I say: what we have presented before is a transmitted explanation (tafsir ma'thur), which the accepted Sunnah has expressed and which the majority have taken. There is nothing in it that prevents the intention of a meaning that corresponds to the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul), agrees with the context of the noble composition and its sequence. This is by saying: after He, the Mighty and Majestic, described the Qur'an in terms that show the greatness of its status and the might of its position, and indicated that it includes what purifies souls and adorns them with what brings their perfection, such as true beliefs and the like, He said, glory be to Him: ﴿A revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾. Thus He, may He be exalted, referred to His own Essence, glory be to Him, by the word "Lord" (Rabb), which indicates nurture (tarbiyya), and nurture is conveying a thing to its perfection gradually, step by step.

This may also be derived from describing it as "noble" (karim), on the basis that the intended meaning is one who is beneficial, abundant in benefits, for there is no benefit more exalted than what has been mentioned. The Mighty and Majestic had mentioned, not far back, what indicates that He, may He be exalted, is the One who sends down the water of rain, and no other, glory be to Him, either independently or jointly. He, the Mighty, said: ﴿Then is it on this Qur'an, of such great standing, containing true beliefs, guiding you to what is beneficial for you, that you are lax, and do not thank Allah for it, and make your thanks into denying it?﴾ And among that is that when you are given rain you say, "We were given rain by such-and-such a mansion," and so you attribute the sending down of rain to the stars, though He has guided you more than once to what contradicts this belief, and has shown you that He, the Exalted, is the One who sends down the rain, not the stars nor anything else at all. So what came as an explanation of ﴿that you deny﴾ by ﴿you say: we were given rain by such-and-such a mansion﴾ is only intended to show a kind of denial required by the situation, denial of the Qur'an described with those majestic attributes. That this is in the manner the disbelievers claim is denial of it is something on which no two rams butt heads. This has no artificiality to it.

It may also be said, supposing that "provision" means rain, and that "you deny" means "you deny that it is from Allah, the Exalted, in that you attribute it to the mansions," although I have not found an explicit statement of this in a report that can be relied upon, the meaning is: Then is it on this Qur'an of great standing, which guides to the fact that every blessing is from Him, the Exalted, and no other, and which explicitly declares that He alone sends down the rain, that ﴿you are scornful﴾ (mudhinun), that is, you deny, according to what you have heard from Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Zajjaj. Among that is that you put in place of thanks for the provision of rain which He gives you and sends down for you, your denial that it is from Allah, the Exalted, and your attribution of it to the mansions. The rebuke that follows is based on their denial of the Qur'an, understood from ﴿that you deny﴾ or from His words, glory be to Him, ﴿you are scornful﴾. However, denial of it is in terms of denial of some of what it has spoken, as previously mentioned. The dependence of the meaning of the verse on the report is not an innovation in the noble Qur'an. The relation of the clause ﴿And you make your provision that you deny﴾ as coordinated (ʿatf) with what precedes it is not hidden from one who has understanding. So reflect, and Allah, the Exalted, is the One who grants success in understanding His noble Book.

Al-Mufaddal related from ʿAsim the reading "takdhibun" (you lie), with lightening (takhfif), from al-kadhib (lying). This is their saying about the Qur'an that it is fabrication, and He is far above that. Their saying about the rain, that it is from the mansions, returns to this, because the Qur'an speaks against it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 56, verses 83–85:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then why, when it [the soul] reaches the throat﴾ etc. is a rebuke, as you have heard. This is in view of their denial of what the saying of Exalted is He, ﴿We created you﴾ etc. speaks of, namely the verses indicating that they are under His dominion (malakut), both in respect of their own selves and in respect of their food and drink and the rest of the means of their livelihood. "Lawla" (why not / if only) is for urging, with the display of their helplessness. "Idha" is temporal. "Al-hulqum" is the passage of food (the gullet). The pronoun in "balaghat" refers to "al-nafs" (the soul), since it is understood from the speech even though no mention of it has preceded. What is meant by it is the spirit (ruh) in the sense of the vapour emanating from the heart, not the rational soul (al-nafs al-natiqah), for the latter is not described by what has been mentioned. It seems this is based on the view that the rational soul is immaterial, which is called the "spirit of command" (al-ruh al-amriyyah), and that it is neither inside the body nor outside it, and does not take on the attributes of bodies such as ascending and descending and others, as chosen by Hujjat al-Islam al-Ghazali and a group of the verifying scholars (muhaqqiqun). The position of the Salaf is that the rational soul, which is the spirit referred to by the saying of Exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about the spirit. Say: The spirit is of the command of my Lord﴾ [al-Isra' 85], is a very subtle body that permeates the body in the manner that rose-water permeates a rose, and it is alive in itself, and it is described by going out and entering and other attributes of bodies. Allamah Ibn al-Qayyim has refuted the view of al-Ghazali and those who agree with him with many proofs, which he mentioned in his book al-Ruh. Its description as reaching the throat is clearly apparent on this view.

As for the view of immateriality and non-localization (tahayyuz), it has been said: what is meant is the weakening of the attachment to the body and the nearness of its severance from it. It is as though it were said: "Then why, when the time of severance of the spirit's attachment to the body has come, [and you, O losers, are around its owner] at that time, i.e., at the time when it has reached the throat and arrived there, or when the time of severance of its attachment has come, [do you look on]" at what it suffers of the distresses. It has also been said: "[do you look on]" means "look on at your own state," and its basis is that they know that what has befallen him will befall them too, so it is as though they were witnessing the condition of their own selves; but this is not the right interpretation.

ʿĪsā read "ḥīnaʾidhin" with a kasra on the nūn, following the vowel of the hamza in "idh". ﴿And We are nearer to him﴾, i.e., to the dying one understood from the speech, ﴿than you﴾. The nearness is meant as knowledge, and this is the mention of the cause while meaning the effect, for nearness is the strongest cause of observation and knowledge. Others have said: what is meant is nearness in knowledge and power, i.e., We are nearer to him than all of that is to you, in that you do not know of his state except what you witness of the signs of severity, without being able to comprehend its reality, its manner, or its true causes, nor being able to exert yourselves to repel it except by what does not avail anything; whereas We are those who take full charge of the details of his condition by Our knowledge and Our power, or through the angels of death. ﴿But you do not see﴾, i.e., you do not perceive that We are nearer to him than you, because of your ignorance of Our affairs. You know that the address is to the disbelievers. It has also been said: you do not perceive the reality of what befalls him, with the exception (istidrak) being from "you look on"; and "ibsar" (seeing) is from sight with the eye, used figuratively for perception, or it is from insight with the heart. It has also been said: what is meant by His nearness to him than them is the nearness of His messengers, Mighty and Majestic is He, i.e., Our messengers who take his soul and endeavour to bring it out are nearer to him than you, but you do not see them.
