Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 56, verse 86:

﴿Then why, if you are not to be brought under authority,﴾ That is, not subject to lordship (marbubin), from dāna (dāna al-sultān al-ra'iyyata), meaning the ruler governed his subjects and held them in servitude (ta'abbadahum). From this it is said of a male slave, madīn, and of a female slave, madīna. Al-Akhtal said:

Her hand raised him, and he grew in her lap, the son of a slave-woman, whom you see, upon his staff, leaning and walking with difficulty.

The statement refers to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is We who created you, so why do you not believe?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 57]. It has also been said that it is from dāna meaning "submitted and humbled himself," and it was used metaphorically for recompense, as in their saying: "As you judge, so you will be judged" (kamā tadīnu tudān), that is: then why, if you are not to be recompensed (majziyyīna)? It was taken to refer to their denial of resurrection. But this is not correct.

﴿Turjiʿūnahā﴾ (you return it), that is, the soul (rūḥ) to its place of settlement. Those who hold that the soul is immaterial (al-qāʾilūna bi'l-tajarrud) say: that is, you return its attachment (taʿalluq) to the body as it was at first.

صفحة 159

﴿in kuntum ṣādiqīn﴾ (if you are truthful) in your belief that He, exalted is He, is not the Creator of it. Their not affirming His creation, glorified is He, is for them an expression of their affirming its non-existence according to their doctrine. In al-Baḥr and others: "in kuntum ṣādiqīn" means: if you are truthful in your denial (taʿṭīl) and your disbelief in the Giver of life, the Giver of death, the Originator and the Restorer, and in your attributing the sending down of rain to the stars (anwāʾ) rather than to Him, mighty and majestic.

The verb turjiʿūn, mentioned here, is the governor (ʿāmil) of the temporal particle idhā in ﴿idhā balaghat al-ḥulqūm﴾ (when it reaches the throat). It is the thing being urged (al-muḥaḍḍaḍ ʿalayhi) by the first lawlā (why not / if not). The second lawlā is a repetition for emphasis. The first lawlā, together with what is within its scope, is the indicator (dalīl) of the answer to the first conditional, namely ﴿in kuntum ghayra madīnīn﴾ (if you are not subject to judgment). The second condition confirms the first and clarifies it. One of the two conditions has been placed before ﴿turjiʿūnahā﴾ for emphasis. The estimated sense is: "Why, then, do you not return it when it reaches the throat, if you are not governed (ghayra marbūbīn) and truthful in what you claim of false belief?" Why, then, do you not return it when it reaches the throat?

The total meaning is: if you are not governed (marbūbīn) as your sayings and deeds require, then why do you not return the soul to the body when it reaches the throat, and send it back as it was, by your power, or by means of some treatment of the natural constitution (ʿilāj li'l-ṭabīʿa)?

His words, exalted is He: ﴿wa-antum ḥīnaʾidhin tanẓurūn﴾ (and you, at that time, are looking on) is a circumstantial clause (jumla ḥāliyya) from the subject of (balaghat). A nominal clause linked by the waw does not need a pronoun for connection, since the waw suffices. So there is no need to say that the returning element is what the tanwīn in ḥīnaʾidhin includes, because the tanwīn is a substitute (ʿiwaḍ) for a clause. That is: "Why do you not return it at the time it reaches the throat, while you are looking at it and at what it suffers of the terror of death-agony, together with your compassion for it and your eagerness to save it from perils?"

His words, glorified is He: ﴿wa-naḥnu aqrabu﴾ (and We are nearer) etc. is a parenthetical interjection (iʿtirāḍ) that reinforces what the speech was brought for, namely rebuking them for what has proceeded from them that indicates the corruption of their belief concerning their Lord, glorified is He. Whether it may be taken as a circumstantial clause is a matter of dispute.

Abū al-Baqāʾ said: ﴿turjiʿūnahā﴾ is the answer to the first lawlā, and this answer dispenses with an answer to the second. It has also been said: the reverse of that.

It has been said: ﴿in kuntum﴾ is a conditional that enters upon another conditional, so the second is put first in the estimated sense — that is: "if you are truthful, if you are not governed, then return the souls to the bodies." What we mentioned earlier is the preference of Jār Allāh (al-Zamakhsharī). In any case, the words of Exalted Allah:

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 56, verses 88–89:**

﴿Then, if he was among those brought near﴾ to the end of the verse. This begins an account of the condition of the deceased after death, following the account of his condition at the moment of death. The pronoun in (kāna) refers to "the deceased" understood from what came before. That is, "if the deceased whose condition was described was among the foremost (al-sābiqīn) of the three groups of spouses," and they are described by their most exalted attributes. ﴿Then rest﴾, meaning: for him there is rest, with ﴿rest﴾ being a mubtada' (subject) whose khabar (predicate) is omitted and placed before it, because it is indefinite. It has also been said that it is the khabar of an omitted mubtada', meaning: "then his recompense is rest," that is, ease. The fa' (then) falls in the response to amma (as for). Some of the eminent scholars said: the sense of this statement is "whatever may be the case, then rest, etc., if he was among those brought near." So "whatever may be the case" was omitted and amma was put in its place. It was not fitting for the fa' to directly follow amma, so a separation was made between amma and the fa' by the Exalted's words ﴿if he was among those brought near﴾ for the sake of the elegance of the expression, just as separation between them occurs by an adverb or an object. The fa' in ﴿then rest﴾ and its two companions is the response to amma, not to (in). Abu al-Baqa' said: the response to amma is ﴿then rest﴾, and as for (in), it is dispensed with by the response to amma, since it is often omitted. In al-Bahr it is stated that when two conditions are combined, the response belongs to the first of them and the response of the second is omitted. So the response here belongs to amma, and this is the position of Sibawayh.

Al-Farisi held that what is mentioned is the response to (in), and the response to amma is omitted. He also had another view that agrees with the position of Sibawayh.

Al-Akhfash held that what is mentioned is a response to both together. We have refuted both positions in the commentary on al-Tashil (Sharh al-Tashil). End of quotation. The well-known view is that the word amma must be attached to the conditional clause. According to al-Radi and a group of scholars, this is the more common usage for this verse. Those who hold the first view said: it is to be understood as "as for the deceased, if he was...". This was objected to on the grounds that it is not hidden that the supposition is unnecessary and that there is no evidence for it except the regularity of the ruling. Furthermore, that amma stands in the place of "whatever may be the case" is generally the case but not universal, as in the phrase "as for Quraysh, I am the best of them," where the sense is "whatever you mention of Quraysh, I am the best of them." The full discussion of this point is to be sought in books of Arabic grammar.

Al-Imam Ahmad, al-Bukhari in his History, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), and others narrated from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recite "fa-rawhun" with a ḍamma on the rā'. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Nuh al-Qari, al-Dahhak, al-Ashhab, Shu'ayb, Sulayman al-Taymi, al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham, Muhammad ibn 'Ali, Abu 'Imran al-Jawni, al-Kalbi, Fayyad, 'Ubayd, and 'Abd al-Warith (from Abu 'Amr), Ya'qub ibn Hassan, Zayd, Ruways (from him), and al-Hasan also recited it so. He said: "al-rūḥ" means mercy, because it is like life to the one who is shown mercy, or it is a cause of his everlasting life. So applying it to mercy is by way of metaphor (isti'ara) or metonymy (majaz mursal). This was also related from Qatada.

Ibn Jinni said: the meaning of this reading returns to the meaning of al-rūḥ, as if it were said: "then for him is the one who holds the spirit (mumsik rūḥ)," and the one who holds it is the spirit itself, just as you say, "the air is life" and "this hearing is living." Some interpreters explained al-rawḥ with a fatḥa as also meaning mercy, as in the Exalted's words ﴿and do not despair of the mercy of Allah﴾ [Yusuf: 87]. It has been said that with a ḍamma it means remaining (al-baqa'). ﴿And fragrance﴾, that is, provision, as related from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak. In another narration from al-Dahhak, it means ease. 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from al-Hasan that he said: it is this basil (rayḥān), that is, the known plant.

Ibn Jarir narrated from him that he said: the soul of the believer leaves his body in a sprig of basil, then he recited ﴿if he was among those brought near﴾, etc.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu al-'Aliya that he said: none of those brought near would depart this world until two branches of the basil of Paradise were brought to him, which he would smell, and then he would be taken (in death). ﴿And a garden of bliss﴾, that is, possessing delight. The annexation (idafa) is of the lam type, or of the least degree of association. This is a reference to the station of those brought near, such that it necessarily follows that they are possessors of bliss.

Al-Imam Ahmad in al-Zuhd, Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham that he said regarding the Exalted's words ﴿if he was among those brought near﴾ ﴿then rest and fragrance﴾: this is for him at the time of death. And regarding the Exalted's words ﴿and a garden of bliss﴾: Paradise is kept hidden for him until the day he is raised. Let it be considered what is meant by "fragrance" according to this view. There is also a statement from some of the early scholars that implies that all of it is in the Hereafter.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 56, verses 88–89:**

﴿Then, if he was among those brought near﴾ to the end of the verse. This begins an account of the condition of the deceased after death, following the account of his condition at the moment of death. The pronoun in (kāna) refers to "the deceased" understood from what came before. That is, "if the deceased whose condition was described was among the foremost (al-sābiqīn) of the three groups of spouses," and they are described by their most exalted attributes. ﴿Then rest﴾, meaning: for him there is rest, with ﴿rest﴾ being a mubtada' (subject) whose khabar (predicate) is omitted and placed before it, because it is indefinite. It has also been said that it is the khabar of an omitted mubtada', meaning: "then his recompense is rest," that is, ease. The fa' (then) falls in the response to amma (as for). Some of the eminent scholars said: the sense of this statement is "whatever may be the case, then rest, etc., if he was among those brought near." So "whatever may be the case" was omitted and amma was put in its place. It was not fitting for the fa' to directly follow amma, so a separation was made between amma and the fa' by the Exalted's words ﴿if he was among those brought near﴾ for the sake of the elegance of the expression, just as separation between them occurs by an adverb or an object. The fa' in ﴿then rest﴾ and its two companions is the response to amma, not to (in). Abu al-Baqa' said: the response to amma is ﴿then rest﴾, and as for (in), it is dispensed with by the response to amma, since it is often omitted. In al-Bahr it is stated that when two conditions are combined, the response belongs to the first of them and the response of the second is omitted. So the response here belongs to amma, and this is the position of Sibawayh.

Al-Farisi held that what is mentioned is the response to (in), and the response to amma is omitted. He also had another view that agrees with the position of Sibawayh.

Al-Akhfash held that what is mentioned is a response to both together. We have refuted both positions in the commentary on al-Tashil (Sharh al-Tashil). End of quotation. The well-known view is that the word amma must be attached to the conditional clause. According to al-Radi and a group of scholars, this is the more common usage for this verse. Those who hold the first view said: it is to be understood as "as for the deceased, if he was...". This was objected to on the grounds that it is not hidden that the supposition is unnecessary and that there is no evidence for it except the regularity of the ruling. Furthermore, that amma stands in the place of "whatever may be the case" is generally the case but not universal, as in the phrase "as for Quraysh, I am the best of them," where the sense is "whatever you mention of Quraysh, I am the best of them." The full discussion of this point is to be sought in books of Arabic grammar.

Al-Imam Ahmad, al-Bukhari in his History, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), and others narrated from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recite "fa-rawhun" with a ḍamma on the rā'. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Nuh al-Qari, al-Dahhak, al-Ashhab, Shu'ayb, Sulayman al-Taymi, al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham, Muhammad ibn 'Ali, Abu 'Imran al-Jawni, al-Kalbi, Fayyad, 'Ubayd, and 'Abd al-Warith (from Abu 'Amr), Ya'qub ibn Hassan, Zayd, Ruways (from him), and al-Hasan also recited it so. He said: "al-rūḥ" means mercy, because it is like life to the one who is shown mercy, or it is a cause of his everlasting life. So applying it to mercy is by way of metaphor (isti'ara) or metonymy (majaz mursal). This was also related from Qatada.

Ibn Jinni said: the meaning of this reading returns to the meaning of al-rūḥ, as if it were said: "then for him is the one who holds the spirit (mumsik rūḥ)," and the one who holds it is the spirit itself, just as you say, "the air is life" and "this hearing is living." Some interpreters explained al-rawḥ with a fatḥa as also meaning mercy, as in the Exalted's words ﴿and do not despair of the mercy of Allah﴾ [Yusuf: 87]. It has been said that with a ḍamma it means remaining (al-baqa'). ﴿And fragrance﴾, that is, provision, as related from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak. In another narration from al-Dahhak, it means ease. 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from al-Hasan that he said: it is this basil (rayḥān), that is, the known plant.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 56, verse 90–91:

﴿And as for if he is of the companions of the right hand﴾ He is referred to by the previous title (ʿunwān), since no other description has been mentioned for them earlier that would indicate their state, as was mentioned for the two latter groups. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Peace be upon you from the companions of the right hand﴾. It has been said: it is on the presumption of a verb of saying (taqdīr al-qawl), meaning: it is said to that one among them who has died, "Peace be upon you, O companion of the right hand, from your brethren, the companions of the right hand," i.e., they greet you, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They will not hear therein any vain speech or sinful utterance﴾ ﴿except the saying "Peace, peace"﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 25, 26]. Thus the address is to the companion of the right hand, and there is no shift (iltifāt) in it given the presumption of a verb of saying. ("Min") here is for the starting point (li-l-ibtidāʾ), as you say, "Peace from so-and-so upon so-and-so," and "Peace to so-and-so from him."

Al-Tabari said: its meaning is "Peace be upon you, you are from the companions of the right hand." So "min aṣḥāb al-yamīn" is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the statement is also on the presumption of a verb of saying. It seems that this explanation is taken from the words of Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him that he said regarding this: The angels come to him from Allah, exalted is He, greeting him and informing him that he is from the companions of the right hand. The apparent meaning is that this is in this sense at death, and that it is in the previous sense in Paradise.

It is also permissible that the meaning is: "Safety is yours from what occupies the heart concerning them, for they are in goodness," i.e., be free of mind concerning them; their affair should not concern you. This is like saying to someone whose heart is attached to his absent son and whose thought is troubled, not knowing his condition: "Be free of mind regarding your son, for he is in ease and comfort." The address is to whoever is fit for it, or to the master of those addressed, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Accordingly, it has been said: it is permissible that this is a consolation to him, peace and blessings be upon him, in the sense that they are not in need of intercession or anything else. However, it is not hidden that the claim that all the companions of the right hand are not in need of what has been mentioned is not established, since intercession for the people of grave sins is a established matter according to the Ahl al-Sunnah. And it is not permissible that they be from the companions of the left; the explicit verses state that they are disbelievers: "They will have no intercessor and no friend who is obeyed." Their being from the companions of the right hand is closer than their being from the foremost, and making them a separate category—you have known its condition, so take heed, for there is nothing in the covenant of antiquity.

Some of the eminent scholars mentioned that this sentence is a statement conveying the greatness of their state, as one says, "So-and-so, it is enough to have him (nāhīka bihi)," and "Your sufficiency is that he is so-and-so," indicating that he is praised beyond the limit of detail. It seems to me you would choose this, for it is fine and subtle.

And as for if he is among the deniers, the astray: ﴿And as for if he is among the deniers, the astray﴾. They are the companions of the left. He described them by this description, as He described them when explaining their states in His words, ﴿Then indeed you, O astray deniers﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 51], as a reproach to them and an indication of the reason for the punishment they were afflicted with. Since this statement came after the denial had been fully established and refuted in the most complete manner, and the preceding statement was not like this, the description of denial was placed first here, contrary to what came before. It is also permissible to say, on the basis that the scope of the object of denial is general, so that it includes his (ﷺ) denial of the claim to prophethood, that this statement is information from Him, glory be to Him, about the states of the three groups. The Prophet (upon him be prayers and peace) was not commanded to address each sentence of it to those it concerns. Therefore the description of denial was placed first in it, encompassing the denial of him (upon him be prayers and peace), which indicates the reason for being afflicted with punishment, as an honour for him (ﷺ) and an exaltation of his high station. And since the preceding statement was within the scope of the speech which he (upon him be prayers and peace) was commanded to address to those disbelievers, it would not be appropriate to place it first for honour, since then it would be of the type of one who praises himself, ("He conveys peace to you"). It is also permissible to say that the statement concerns the state of the disbelieving dying person, and denial, being the opposite of belief, can only be in the heart, and the heart is not disabled as the other limbs are disabled. Therefore it was placed first here. This is indicated by what they have said in the supplication of the funeral prayer (salat al-janazah, the Islamic funeral prayer): "O Allah, whomever of us You keep alive, keep him upon Islam, and whomever of us You cause to die, cause him to die upon faith," in that Islam is specified for life and faith for death.

The Imam said regarding this: The meaning of error (al-dalal) there is what proceeded from them of persistence upon the great sin, so they went astray from the way of Allah, the Exalted, and did not reach it. Then they denied His messengers. ﴿They say, "When we have died…"﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 82], etc., so they denied the resurrection. Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿O astray ones﴾, who associated others with Allah, the deniers, who denied the gathering, "you will surely eat of the bitter tree" (and so on). As for here, He, glory be to Him, said to them: "O deniers, who denied the gathering, the astray from the path of deliverance, who are not guided to bliss." There is another aspect to this, which is that the address there is with the disbelievers, so He, glory be to Him, said: "O you who associated others with Allah first and denied second." And the address here is with the Prophet (may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him), explaining to him (upon him be prayers and peace) the state of the three groups, as indicated by ﴿So peace be to you﴾. Then He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿As for those brought near, there is rest and bounty and a garden of delight. And as for the companions of the right, peace be to you from the companions of the right﴾, and as for the deniers who denied you and went astray, He placed their denial first, as an indication of the honour of him (may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him), since he made clear that the strongest cause of their punishment is their denial. End.

And you should reflect with fairness and examine what was said, rather than looking at who said it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 56, verses 93–94:

And His saying, ﴿Then a welcome (nuzul)﴾ is by way of an elision: "Then for him is a welcome (nuzul)," or "Then his recompense is a welcome (nuzul), existing ﴿of boiling water﴾." It has been said: he drinks after eating the zaqqum, as was detailed earlier. ﴿And burning in Hellfire﴾ means being made to enter the Fire. It has also been said: it means remaining in it and suffering its various kinds of torment. All of this is based on the view that the intent is to describe what they will have on the Day of Resurrection. It has also been said: this is to be understood as what he finds in the grave of the heat of the Fire and its smoke, because the discussion concerns the time of death and immediately after the taking of souls, and what is most fitting for this is that what is mentioned belongs to the barzakh (intermediate state).

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said concerning the verse: "The disbeliever will not leave [the grave] until he drinks a cup of boiling water."

Ahmad ibn Musa, al-Minqari and al-Lu'lu'i reported from Abu ʿAmr the reading ﴿wa-tasliyati﴾ with a kasra, as a conjunction (ʿatf) on ( ḥamim ).

This is the commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 56, verse 95:

﴿Indeed, this﴾, that is, what has been mentioned in the noble surah, as Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, ﴿is the certainty of certainty (haqq al-yaqin)﴾. Al-yaqin (certainty), as is understood from the words of al-Zamakhshari in (the commentary on) Surah al-Jathiyah, is a name for knowledge from which doubt has been removed. The author of al-Mat'a (Sahib al-Mat'a) explicitly stated this and mentioned that it is an explanation according to meaning, and that it is derived from the context. Otherwise, it simply means certain knowledge in absolute terms. The idafah (genitive construction) is in the sense of "min" or "al-", and the meaning is: ﴿it is the very essence of certainty (ayn al-yaqin)﴾. It is like the essence of a thing and its self. It is not hidden that the idafah is from the idafah of the general to the specific, and that it being in the sense of "al-" is the view of some scholars. Another group said: it is explicative (bayaniyyah) in the sense of "min". Some scholars here supposed a qualified noun, meaning: it is truly the certainty of the report (haqq al-khabar al-yaqin), and that this does not fit the context is not a valid objection. In al-Bahr it is said: it has been said that the idafah is from the idafah of two synonyms for the sake of emphasis, just as you say "this is the certainty of certainty" and "the correctness of correctness," meaning that it is the utmost in that matter. Thus the two are of one meaning, one being annexed to the other for emphasis. In this there is consideration.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 56, verse 96:

The *fa'* in His saying, ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾, indicates the sequence of the glorification or the command to it, since the truth of what has been detailed within this noble surah, which necessitates glorifying Him above what is unbefitting, from what the disbelievers attribute to Him, whether by statement or by state, exalted is He far above that, is established. Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, and others, related from Uqba ibn Amir al-Juhani, who said: "When the verse ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾ was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he said: 'Make it in your bowing (ruku').' And when ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ was revealed, he said: 'Make it in your prostration (sujud).'"

"Among what the masters, the people of allusion (arbab al-ishara, the Sufi masters), have said" concerning some of this noble surah is that "the Waqi'ah" (the Inevitable Event) is a name for the resurrection of the spirit (ruh), just as "al-Azifah" (the Imminent Event) is a name for the resurrection of the hidden (khafi), "al-Haqqah" (the Sure Reality) is a name for the resurrection of the innermost secret (sirr), and "al-Sa'ah" (the Hour) is a name for the resurrection of the heart (qalb). They said: When the Waqi'ah occurs, it raises its companion at one time and lowers him at another, kindles the fires of zeal, bursts forth the rivers of gnosis (ma'rifah), and it comes to the wayfarer (salik) when he occupies himself with the spiritual path (suluk) and purification (tasfiyah), and his remembrance (dhikr) reaches the spirit. At the beginning it is like a black curtain that comes from above the head when the remembrance overwhelms, and whenever it descends further, awe (haybah) and tranquility (sakinah) fall upon the one who remembers. Perhaps at the beginning he faints, and when it falls upon his eyes he witnesses the worlds of the unseen, so he sees what Allah the Exalted wills him to see, the spiritual sciences are unveiled to him, and he sees wonders and marvels without number. When he regains consciousness, he should present what has occurred to him to his guide (mashlak), so that he may direct him to what is beneficial for his time, interpret for him what is suitable to his capacity (hawsalah), strengthen his heart, and command him to remembrance and total devotion, until he becomes perfected with the pure essence of the Waqi'ah and becomes an illuminated secret. Perhaps the wayfarer reaches a state where, when he opens his eyes after its descent in the world of witnessing (alam al-shahadah), he sees what he was witnessing in it. This is a lofty and esteemed state among the people of the spiritual path. Therefore its occurrence is not a lie; rather it is true, because Satan flees from it and the self (nafs) cannot deceive its companion through it. It is the true wakefulness, and what people consider wakefulness is sleep, as indicated by the saying of the Commander of the Faithful, Ali, may Allah ennoble his face: "People are asleep; when they die, they awaken."

Then they spoke about most of what is in this glorious surah in terms relating to the souls (anfus). They also said, regarding the "positions of the stars" (mawaqi' al-nujum), that they are an indication of the purified subtleties (latha'if), because they are the positions of the stars of the sacred inspirations (al-waridat al-qudsiyyah) that are hidden from the heaven of Jabarut and Lahut. It has been said: In His saying, ﴿None touches it except the purified﴾, there is an indication that it is not fitting for one whose soul is not pure from the state of inclination (hadath al-mayl) to minor desires (saghair al-shahawat), which is the minor impurity (al-hadath al-asghar), and from the state of inclination to major desires (kaba'ir al-shahawat), which is the major impurity (al-hadath al-akbar), to touch with the hand of his self and his thought the meanings of the Noble Qur'an, just as it is not fitting for one who is not pure in body from the two well-known impurities in the body to touch with the hand of his body and his flesh its written words. It has also been said that it is permissible to say that the meaning is: "None reaches even the lowest of the realities of the secrets of the Noble Qur'an except the purified from the filth of desires and the impurities of transgressions."

If this sentence is a description of the "Hidden Book," meaning by it the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), and by "the purified" the angels, peace be upon them, and the meaning is that none has knowledge of it except the angels, peace be upon them, then this constitutes a refutation of those who claim that the saints (awliya') see the Preserved Tablet and become aware of what is in it. However, interpreting "the purified" as including the angels and the saints whose souls have been purified and whose essences have been sanctified, until they have joined the angels, peace be upon them, is not beneficial in discussion with the people of the Shari'ah, since their proofs for the legal rulings rest on the apparent meanings. Moreover, it has not been reported from the Prophet (ﷺ), and he is who he is, that he looked one day while among his companions at the Preserved Tablet and became aware of something in it, and said to them: "I have seen the Preserved Tablet and become aware of such and such in it." Likewise, it has not been reported from the eminent companions, the Rightly Guided Caliphs, that this happened to them, and disputes arose among them concerning matters about which they differed, and their contention over verifying them lasted until the crescent of truth was nearly obscured, yet none of them consulted the Preserved Tablet to unveil them.

Some scholars have mentioned that the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary (sidrat al-muntaha) is where the knowledge of those beneath it ends, and that the Tablet is far above it. Both of these have been expressed in reports, and this indicates that the saints do not become aware of the Tablet. Despite all this, whoever claims that the awareness has occurred, upon him is the proof, and how can he produce it? What you have heard is based on what the reports have stated about the description of the Preserved Tablet, that it is a physical body in which was written what has been and what will be until the Day of Resurrection. But if something other than that is said about it, the discussion extends beyond what you have heard, and the circle widens.

Among that is their saying: The Tablets are four: the Tablet of the Preceding Decree (lawh al-qada' al-sabiq), which is prior to erasure and affirmation, and it is the Tablet of the First Intellect (al-'aql al-awwal); the Tablet of Destiny (lawh al-qadar), that is, the Tablet of the universal rational soul (al-nafs al-natiqah al-kulliyyah), in which the universals of the First Tablet are detailed, and it is what is called the Preserved Tablet; the Tablet of the particular celestial soul (al-nafs al-juz'iyyah al-samawiyyah), in which is imprinted everything in this world, its form, its configuration and its measure, and it is what is called the lowest heaven (al-sama' al-dunya), and it is in the position of the imagination (khayal) of the world, just as the first is in the position of its spirit and the second in the position of its heart; and the Tablet of prime matter (hayula), which receives the form in the world of witnessing. They also say other things, and the advocate of this position recites his saying:

*"And when you do not see the crescent, then submit to people who saw it with their eyes."*

Moreover, do not think that denying their seeing the Preserved Tablet is a denial of their unveiling miracles (karamat kashfiyyah) and their unseen inspirations (ilhamat ghaybiyyah) — far be it from Allah the Exalted! The means by which Allah the Exalted informs whomever He wills of His saints about whatever He wills of His knowledge are not restricted to showing them the Preserved Tablet. Furthermore, the possibility of this is not disputed; the discussion is only about its occurrence and its transmission from the Prophet (ﷺ) and the eminent companions, such as as-Siddiq, al-Faruq, Dhu al-Nurayn, the Gate of the City of Knowledge, and the dot beneath the ba' (al-nuqtah allati tahta al-ba'), may Allah the Exalted be pleased with them all. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

Concerning His saying, ﴿And We are nearer to Him than you, but you do not see﴾, they built their interpretation on the doctrine of the unity of existence (wahdat al-wujud), and the discussion of it is widespread, and we have pointed to it in this book more than once. They have various expressions regarding certainty (yaqin), the eye of certainty (ayn al-yaqin) and the truth of certainty (haqq al-yaqin). Among them: Certainty is the vision of direct sight by the strength of faith, not by argument and proof. It has also been said: It is the witnessing of the unseen by the purity of hearts, and the observing of secrets by the preservation of thoughts. It has been said: It is the tranquility of the heart upon the reality of a thing, from "yaqana al-ma'" (the water became still) when it settles in the pool. The truth of certainty is the annihilation (fana') of the servant in the Real and his subsistence in Him, in knowledge, witnessing and state, not knowledge alone. So the knowledge of every rational person of death is the knowledge of certainty; when he sees the angels, it is the eye of certainty; and when he tastes death, it is the truth of certainty. It has been said: The knowledge of certainty is the outward Shari'ah, the eye of certainty is sincerity (ikhlas) in it, and the truth of certainty is witnessing within it. "It has been said: It has been said." We ask Allah the Exalted for guidance to the most upright path, and that He expand our breasts with the lights of the sciences of His Noble and Glorious Book. He, glorified is He, is sufficient for us in both abodes, and how excellent a Guardian He is.
